docs.title: Description
docs.text:
PREFFECT (PaRaffin Embedded Formalin-FixEd Cleaning Tool) is a probabilistic framework for the analysis of RNA sequencing data from formalin-fixed paraffin embedded (FFPE) samples. PREFFECT uses generative models to fit distributions to observed expression measurements while adjusting for technical and biological variables. PREFFECT offers a series of models that exploit multiple expression profiles generated from matched tissues for a single sample, sample-sample adjacency networks and clinicopathological/technical sample variables.

PREFFECT is designed to accomplish the following tasks:

  • Accurately denoise RNAseq data from FFPE materials (fRNAseq)
  • Impute missing values from the count matrix
  • Improve performance of standard analyses

docs.title: Where to go
docs.text:
• Getting started installs it and fits a model.
  • The command line is every command and every option, with what each is for and when to change it.
  • The graphical interface prepares and looks at a folder of counts, applies a saved model and shows the figures a page at a time, in a browser, on your own machine.
  • Using it covers the real workflow: checking data, choosing genes, imputing, clustering, drawing.
  • Reference is the API, taken from the docstrings.
  • What changed from 0.1

docs.title: A note on this version
docs.text: Version 0.2 is a rewrite, not a patch. CHANGELOG.md lists every fix and change relative to version 0.1, and opens with how to tell which of them explains a difference in your results.

docs.title: What changed from version 0.1
docs.text: This page is the summary. The point-form list of every fix, opening with how to tell which one explains a difference between your version 0.1 and version 0.2 results, is CHANGELOG.md in the repository. The experiment folders named exp/NN and the decision records mentioned below belong to the development record, which is not part of this release.

docs.title: The ones that move a number
docs.text:
The network term weights the linked pairs against the absent ones. Version 0.1 scored the predicted sample-sample network against the observed one with a plain mean over every pair, and carried a weight for present edges and one for absent edges that nothing set. On a network one per cent dense that is 99 parts "no edge here" to one part "edge here", and measured on synthetic data with a known network, the network half of the model learned nothing under it: the decoder settled on predicting no edge anywhere and the network latent collapsed onto its prior, in every seed. The linked pairs now carry the same total weight as the absent ones, which on that synthetic network recovers its structure as well as a predictor that knows the sample groups, in six seeds of six, with clustering, imputation and the expression terms unchanged. On the two datasets run since, the DCIS cohort in exp/17 and dataset_full_1 in exp/18, the balanced term did not recover a network: on the first every arm's decoder ended at exactly one half for every pair, and on the second every decoder predicted no edge anywhere. Nothing measured is worse under it, which is why it stays the default. --edge-balance none gives the old term, for repeating a result produced under it. Decision of 2026-10-30.

The objective is one list of named terms. Version 0.1 kept two hand-written lists, a numerator and a divisor, and they disagreed: a term was computed, weighted, logged, and then left out of the sum while its weight stayed in the divisor. The total and the divisor are now derived from the same list, so they cannot disagree.

Per-tissue weights are checked, not truncated. Version 0.1 paired weights against losses with zip, which stops at the shorter, so a two-tissue run with a one-entry weight list dropped the second tissue out of the objective. A list of the wrong length now raises and names every offending weight.

The reported validation loss is a mean. Version 0.1 divided by the number of tissues rather than the number of batches, so with six validation batches the figure was six times the mean and not comparable across batch sizes.

The last partial batch of each epoch is kept. Version 0.1 discarded it.

Inference uses the latent mean. Version 0.1 ran inference through the training path, which samples, so the same model over the same data gave different cleaned counts every time.

Two rectifiers were removed, one on the latent parameters and one after the decoder. Neither changes what the model reconstructs. These were decided on synthetic data at 150 genes and the decision records say so.

The encoder is fed log(1 + counts). Version 0.1 fed it raw counts, which reach millions in a real cohort, so an ordinary training step could move the encoder's output a thousandfold at once: the loss spikes of issue #22. On the log scale the spikes are gone in every seed measured, imputation error more than halves and clustering recovery more than doubles. What the model predicts, and the scale it is scored on, are unchanged. Measured on the simple model and on the one-tissue graph model, with the same result on both, and measured again on 2026-11-02 under the corrected library size, which left the result standing.

The library size is corrected for entries a mask hid. A sample's library size is its total count, and the model multiplies everything it predicts for that sample by it. Both versions read that total off the counts the model was shown, which under a mask is short by the hidden fraction while the counts the model is scored against are not, so every expected count came out short by the same fraction and nothing in the model could recover it. The total is now estimated back from how many of a sample's entries were hidden, never from their values. Measured on synthetic counts with no zeros, a fifth hidden: the expected counts went from 0.801 of the true grand total to 1.001. A run without hidden entries is bit for bit what it was, so nothing apply produces for a real cohort moves. What it does to a reported imputation error depends on how well the composition was fitted and is not one factor. The end-to-end comparison of the two versions was measured again on 2026-11-02 with both of them corrected, version 0.2 inside its model and version 0.1 as its stored predictions are scored, and it left every verdict standing. Finding 56.

The full model trains. Until 2026-11-02 it could be built, run forward and scored, but train stopped at its first batch, because the loop asked every batch a question only a single-tissue one answers. All three models now train from Python and from the command line, and the suite trains each of them. Finding 55.

A patient missing one tissue is padded, and the padding is accounted for. Version 0.1 kept such a patient and filled the tissue they lacked with the rounded per-gene mean of the real samples, a row it called a ghost. Version 0.2 refused them outright until 2026-11-02 and now does what version 0.1 did, rule for rule, with three things version 0.1 left implicit made explicit: the data carries which rows are padding rather than recovering it from a name beginning tau_, a mask that would hide an entry in a padded row is refused rather than silently skipped, and infer and apply drop padded rows from their output and say how many. preffect check reports how many patients lack each tissue before anything is fitted. A cohort with nothing to pad trains and scores exactly as it did. The decision of 2026-11-02 on unmatched samples has the measurement against the alternative, which is dropping those patients.

docs.title: The ones that stop you doing something
docs.text:
These make a class of mistake impossible rather than changing a result.

  • A model kind that cannot be honoured raises. Version 0.1 silently turned a request for the graph model into the plain one, loaded the network, and ignored it.
  • imputation_error requires truth. Version 0.1 invented it as the per-gene mean when it was absent.
  • Gene selection matches by name, never by position, and a panel that matches nothing raises.
  • A sample-sample network with no edges raises. Every dataset version 0.1 shipped carries an identity matrix there (findings 35 and 54), so a graph model on them was ten times the parameters for nothing.
  • The settings are frozen. Version 0.1 had four parts of the code modifying a shared dictionary while it ran.
  • A saved model carries the record of the run that made it: the loss at every epoch for each split, the epoch it stopped at and why, and how long the fitting took. Version 0.1 kept none of it, so a model reopened a week later could be applied, and its figures drawn, with no way to tell whether the fit had finished moving. The graphical interface now describes the run, loss curve included, before it shows a single figure. A model saved before the record was kept says so in a sentence rather than showing nothing.
  • Comparing two fitted models names a winner only above a stated threshold, and says the threshold was chosen rather than measured. One fit of each model cannot say how much of a difference is the seed, which is why this project's own experiments use six of them, and a table that reported the sign of that difference would be reporting noise.
  • A counts or sample table that cannot be opened is refused in a sentence. Both readers handed the file straight to pandas, so a path that was not there arrived as twenty lines of stack ending inside pandas, on the command line and on the page that asks for the path. Finding 66.
  • The example cohort's three splits are drawn from the same genes, and a test fails if the per-gene means of any two of them disagree. Version 0.1's vignettes shipped a test folder that was a copy of the validation folder; version 0.2's first generator avoided that and made the opposite mistake, drawing each split's genes separately, so the splits could not be compared at all and a model fitted on one could say nothing about another. Finding 65.

docs.title: What the package now does that version 0.1 left to you
docs.text: Preparing the input file. Version 0.1 described the layout and left assembling it to each user, and getting it wrong is what most people's first run failed on. preffect prepare builds the file from a counts table and a sample table, including the correspondence table the full model needs, and preffect network adds a sample-sample network to files that have none. Both refuse rather than repair: counts that are not whole numbers name the entries at fault, and a number of neighbours that leaves the network empty or complete is refused. preffect.prepare holds the same functions for use from Python. The network recipe is version 0.1's own as it was meant to work, with the number of neighbours this project measured; no dataset version 0.1 shipped carries a real network at all (findings 35 and 54).

docs.title: What is ported from the paper's own tools
docs.text:
The standalone estimator that decides which distribution a cohort needs. Version 0.1 shipped it as wrappers/_ZINBEstimator.py and the paper used it to establish that the plain negative binomial is enough for fRNA-seq, which is why the plain one is the default here. It is now preffect.zinb_fit, which fits both distributions to one gene's counts and reports which the Akaike information criterion prefers, and which runs over the columns of a matrix in one call.

The likelihood is unchanged and the two versions agree on every set of counts version 0.1 could fit. Three things about the search changed, each because version 0.1 lost fits it should have kept: it varies the dispersion rather than dividing for it afterwards, it starts each search consistently with the amount of zero inflation that search is exploring, and it raises rather than returning nothing. Findings 57, 58 and 60 and the decision of 2026-11-02 on this estimator have the measurements.

Choosing the zero-inflated distribution from the command line. The distribution, the model paths that use it and the loss were all ported and tested, and then there was no way to ask for it: preffect train had no likelihood option until 2026-11-02. Version 0.1 documented model_likelihood: NB | ZINB in its settings page, and nothing recorded a decision to drop it, so it was an omission rather than a choice. It is now preffect train --likelihood {NB,ZINB}, the choice is saved with the model so apply rebuilds the right distribution, and the graphical interface shows which distribution a loaded model was fitted with. Finding 61.

docs.title: What is not ported
docs.text: A differential expression function that version 0.1 itself marks "in development". Transfer learning is ported (--from-model and --freeze on the command line, preffect.pretraining in Python), and it now freezes what it is asked to freeze: version 0.1's version set every part trainable whichever branch ran.

docs.title: Choosing a distribution
docs.text: This page is about deciding, before you train anything, whether your counts need the zero-inflated distribution or whether the plain one is enough. It covers the call that makes the decision, what the numbers mean, where it refuses to answer.

docs.title: The question
docs.text:
PREFFECT can fit counts with either of two distributions. The negative binomial says a gene has an average level and a spread around it wider than pure counting noise. The zero-inflated negative binomial is the same thing plus a separate probability that a count is zero for a reason unrelated to expression level, such as the transcript never being captured.

Adding that probability always fits the data at least as well, because it can be set to nothing and recover the plain distribution. So fitting better is not a reason to use it. The question is whether it fits enough better to be worth the extra parameter, and the Akaike information criterion is the usual way to answer it. The criterion is the fitted log-likelihood penalised by the number of parameters, and the smaller value wins.

The PREFFECT paper asked exactly this question of fRNA-seq counts and found that the plain distribution is usually enough, which is why Likelihood defaults to it. The code here is the estimator that produced that answer, so the evidence can be reproduced and the question asked again of a new cohort.

docs.title: One gene
docs.text:
compare_fits takes one gene's counts across samples and returns both fits with the verdict.

import numpy as np

from preffect.zinb_fit import compare_fits

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)


def draw(mean, dispersion, zero_probability, n=400):
    counts = rng.negative_binomial(
        dispersion, dispersion / (dispersion + mean), size=n
    ).astype(float)
    counts[rng.random(n) < zero_probability] = 0.0
    return counts


plain = draw(mean=30, dispersion=3, zero_probability=0.0)
comparison = compare_fits(plain)

>>> comparison.preferred
'NB'
>>> round(comparison.aic_difference, 2)
-1.33
>>> comparison.negative_binomial
NegativeBinomialFit(mean=30.97750020843003, dispersion=2.754773927681657,
                    log_likelihood=-1701.9800050052718, aic=3407.9600100105436,
                    dispersion_at_bound=False)

The same call on counts that really do have extra zeros:

inflated = draw(mean=30, dispersion=3, zero_probability=0.4)
comparison = compare_fits(inflated)

>>> comparison.preferred, round(comparison.aic_difference, 1)
('ZINB', 306.5)
>>> comparison.zero_inflated
ZeroInflatedFit(mean=30.300878641209515, dispersion=3.418954422277129,
                zero_probability=0.38475435143728937,
                log_likelihood=-1290.230705904805, aic=2586.46141180961,
                dispersion_at_bound=False, starts_converged=8)
>>> comparison.zero_inflated.observed_mean
18.642483731630936

docs.title: Reading the numbers
docs.text:
Four of the reported quantities need saying out loud, because three of them are easy to read as something they are not.

  • aic_difference is the plain fit's criterion minus the zero-inflated one's, so positive means the extra zeros earned their parameter. A difference under 2 means the two fit about equally well. Above 10 the evidence is usually called strong.
  • mean is the mean of the negative binomial component, not of the distribution. Above, the component's mean is 30.3 while the counts themselves average 18.6, because two counts in five were forced to zero. observed_mean is the second number.
  • dispersion is PREFFECT's theta, the inverse dispersion. Large means close to Poisson, small means heavily overdispersed, and the variance is mean + mean**2 / dispersion. A textbook that calls the dispersion alpha means 1 / theta.
  • dispersion_at_bound means the counts are at least as tight as a Poisson, so the dispersion is not identified and what is reported is the largest value the fit allows. This is common on genes with almost no counts and on anything close to constant.

docs.title: A whole matrix
docs.text:
compare_fits_over_columns runs the same comparison down every column of a counts matrix, which is one gene each in a samples-by-genes matrix, and returns a table with one row per gene.

from preffect.zinb_fit import compare_fits_over_columns

matrix = np.column_stack(
    [plain, inflated, draw(5, 1, 0.0), draw(80, 6, 0.6)]
)
table = compare_fits_over_columns(
    matrix, names=["GENE_A", "GENE_B", "GENE_C", "GENE_D"]
)

>>> table[["name", "zero_fraction", "preferred",
...        "aic_difference", "zinb_zero_probability"]].round(3)
     name  zero_fraction preferred  aic_difference  zinb_zero_probability
0  GENE_A          0.002        NB          -1.332                  0.002
1  GENE_B          0.385      ZINB         306.510                  0.385
2  GENE_C          0.188        NB          -1.364                  0.037
3  GENE_D          0.565      ZINB         429.242                  0.565

GENE_C is the row worth looking at. Nearly a fifth of its counts are zero and the plain distribution still wins, because a gene with a mean of 5 and a wide spread produces that many zeros on its own. A high proportion of zeros is not evidence of zero inflation by itself, which is the whole reason for fitting rather than counting.

A DataFrame brings its own column names, so names can be left out when you pass one.

docs.title: Where it refuses to answer
docs.text:
Three situations raise rather than returning a number, because a number would be a guess.

What happened What is raised Why The values are not whole, non-negative, finite numbers DataError A count distribution has no probability to give them. Round the counts yourself if that is what you mean, as the paper's notebooks did. Every count is zero FitError Any mean fits equally well as long as the extra-zero probability is one, so nothing is identified. No search converged FitError There is no fit to report.

In a sweep over thousands of genes, stopping at the first gene that cannot be fitted is the default, because a sweep that quietly drops genes turns a claim about a cohort into a claim about whichever subset happened to fit. Pass on_failure="record" to carry on instead; the reason goes in the row's problem column and its numbers are left missing.

docs.title: How long it takes
docs.text:
Fitting both distributions to one gene across 220 samples takes about 0.18 seconds on one thread. So 2,000 genes take six minutes and a 19,000-gene cohort takes about an hour. Nothing here is on a training path, so it has not been made faster than that.

If you are sweeping a whole cohort, the reason to pass on_failure="record" is that an hour's work should not be thrown away by one gene. Read the problem column afterwards and decide what to do about the rows that have one.

docs.title: Reproducing the paper's comparison
docs.text: The reference values are in tests/data/version_0_1_zinb_fits.json: nine count vectors with the fits the paper's notebooks compared against. tests/test_zinb_fit.py checks the estimator against them.

docs.title: The command line
docs.text:
Six commands, in the order you meet them. The first two turn what your study already has into the files PREFFECT reads, and are needed once; the next three are the work itself. A seventh opens the same work in a browser:

Command What it does preffect prepare builds the tissue files from a counts table and a sample table preffect network adds a sample-sample network to tissue files that have none preffect check reads the counts and says whether they can be used, without fitting anything preffect train fits a model and saves it to one file preffect apply runs a saved model over counts and writes the cleaned result preffect example-data writes a small simulated cohort to try the others on

preffect --help lists the commands, preffect <command> --help lists a command's options with their defaults, and preffect --version prints the version. This page says the same things at more length: what each option is for, and when to change it.

The examples write preffect. If you installed a copy of the source with scripts/install.sh, write .venv/bin/preffect. If preffect is not on your path at all, or prints something you did not expect, python -P -m preffect runs the same thing. -P stops Python putting the current folder first on the import path, so a folder named preffect beside you cannot be mistaken for the installed package.

docs.title: What every command shares
docs.text:
A data folder, not a file. Each of --train, --validation and --data names a folder holding one file per tissue, named <anything>tau_<n>.h5ad with <n> counting from 1. A single-tissue cohort, which is the usual case, has one file ending tau_1.h5ad. Getting started says what has to be inside it.

--tissues is how many of those files to expect. A tissue here is one sample from each patient under one condition, such as tumour and adjacent normal; the full model fits several at once. The default of 1 is right for everything except the full model.

It says what it is doing. Every command prints what it read and what it produced, so a long run that says nothing can be told apart from one that has hung, and a run that produced nothing cannot look like one that succeeded.

It stops rather than guesses. A setting that cannot be honoured, a folder that does not exist, or an output path that cannot be written stops the command with one sentence naming the problem, before any work is done. The exit status is 0 when the command did what was asked, 2 when it refused, and 1 when no command was given. A refusal prints no traceback, because a traceback tells someone who did not write the code nothing they can act on.

docs.title: preffect prepare
docs.text:
Turns a table of counts and a table describing the samples into the files the other commands read. Run it once, when your study's counts are still in whatever a sequencing pipeline wrote.

preffect prepare --counts counts.csv --samples samples.csv --out my_study/train
Option What it does Default --counts a comma- or tab-separated table of counts; give it once per tissue required --samples a table describing those samples, once per tissue, in the same order required --out the folder to write the tissue files in required --counts-are which way round the counts table is written samples-by-genes --sample-column which column of the sample table holds the sample names the first --name what the files are called before the tissue number counts --patient-column which column says which patient a sample came from none --neighbours also build a sample-sample network, with this many links per sample none --mutual keep a link only where each sample is among the other's nearest off --label a column of the sample table to measure the network against none --overwrite write over files already in --out off

The counts are read with one row per sample, the sample names in the first column and the gene names in the first row. A table written the other way round, one row per gene, is common; --counts-are genes-by-samples turns it the right way round. The counts have to be whole numbers that are not negative, and a table that is not says which entries are at fault.

Output on a 60-sample study:

tissue 1: 60 samples and 400 genes from counts.csv, read as samples-by-genes
  3 annotation(s) per sample from samples.csv
  tissue 1: 60 samples, 371 edge(s), 12.4 per sample (fewest 10, middle 11, most 19); no isolated samples
  tissue 1: 100.0% of edges join two samples with the same subtype, against 32.2% if the edges ignored it
wrote my_study/train/counts.tau_1.h5ad
check it with: preffect check --train my_study/train

Several tissues at once, for the full model. Give --counts and --samples once per tissue and name the column that says which patient each sample came from. That column is the only thing linking a sample in one tissue to a sample in another, since the files do not share sample names, and the full model cannot be fitted without it. A patient with no sample in some tissue is kept, with a gap recorded for that tissue, which is the case the full model pads:

tissue 1: 60 samples and 400 genes from counts.csv, read as samples-by-genes
tissue 2: 48 samples and 400 genes from counts_normal.csv, read as samples-by-genes
60 patient(s) across 2 tissues
  tissue 1: every patient has a sample here
  tissue 2: 12 patient(s) have no sample here, and the full model pads a row of per-gene means in for each of them
wrote my_study/full/counts.tau_1.h5ad
wrote my_study/full/counts.tau_2.h5ad

docs.title: preffect network
docs.text:
Builds a sample-sample network from the counts themselves and writes a copy of each tissue file carrying it. Only the single and full models use a network; the simple model does not, and does not need this command.

preffect network --data my_study/train --out my_study/train_linked
Option What it does Default --data the folder of counts to read required --out the folder to write the copies in, under the same file names required --tissues how many tissue files the folder holds 1 --neighbours link each sample to this many others 10 --mutual keep a link only where each sample is among the other's nearest off --label a sample annotation to measure the network against none --replace build a new network for a file that already carries one with links in it off --overwrite write over files already in --out off

The files it reads are left exactly as they are. It writes copies, which is both this project's rule for source data and the only safe thing to do to somebody's only copy.

tissue 1: my_study/train/counts.tau_1.h5ad
  wrote my_study/train_linked/counts.tau_1.h5ad
  60 samples, 371 edge(s), 12.4 per sample (fewest 10, middle 11, most 19); no isolated samples
  100.0% of edges join two samples with the same subtype, against 32.2% if the edges ignored it
the counts are unchanged; fit a graph model on them with preffect train --train my_study/train_linked --kind single

Three lines there are worth reading closely.

  • The links per sample is larger than the number asked for, here 12.4 against 10, because a link is kept wherever either of the two samples names the other. A sample that nothing else names keeps exactly ten.
  • --label is how you find out whether the network carries anything. The second line compares the share of links joining two samples with the same value of that annotation against the share that would do so if the links ignored it. Far above chance means the network found real structure. The two being equal, as in 31.2% ... against 31.9%, means it found none, and a graph model over it will cost ten times the parameters of the simple model for nothing.
  • A sample with no link at all is reported where there is one. It happens with --mutual, and a graph model learns nothing for such a sample.

Where the recipe comes from. Each sample is linked to the ten others whose square-rooted counts correlate with it most. Ten neighbours is the setting measured on this project's cohort: the one network under which the graph model beat the simple model, by 8 per cent lower imputation error at hidden entries.

docs.title: preffect check
docs.text:
Reads the data, reports what it found, and refuses if something would stop a run. It takes seconds and it is the single most useful command here, because the problems it finds otherwise show up as a confusing result rather than as an error.

preffect check --train my_study/train --validation my_study/validation
Option What it does Default --train folder of training counts required --validation folder of validation counts none --tissues how many tissue files each folder holds 1

Output on the vignette data:

training: 1 tissue(s) from vignette_data/simple/train
  tissue 1: 120 samples, 200 genes, no network
  tissue 1: carries the count each entry was drawn from in layers['true_expected_counts'], so these counts are simulated
  the counts look usable
validation: 40 samples from vignette_data/simple/validation
  tissue 1: 0 of 120 training samples reappear in validation

Four lines are worth reading closely.

  • The network. no network means the file carries no sample-sample network, so only the simple model applies. a network with 240 edge(s), 4.0 per sample means the graph models have something to use. a network with NO edges between samples means the file carries a network that links every sample to itself and to nothing else. A graph model on one of those costs ten times the parameters and has nothing to attend to, so train refuses it.
  • The overlap. 0 of 120 training samples reappear in validation is the line that tells you your splits are what you think they are. If every training sample reappears, it says the validation data is the training data. Leave --validation out instead.
  • Without a validation set it says validation: none given, so no validation loss will be reported, and that is all it does. It does not invent one.
  • Simulated data says so. The line about layers['true_expected_counts'] appears only where a file carries the count each entry was drawn from, which only something generated can. It will not appear on your own data. The worked example uses that layer to score filled-in entries against the signal rather than against one noisy draw of it.

With --tissues 2 or more it adds one line per tissue saying how many patients have no sample there:

training: 2 tissue(s) from my_study/train
  tissue 1: 120 samples, 200 genes, a network with 240 edge(s), 4.0 per sample
  tissue 2: 96 samples, 200 genes, a network with 192 edge(s), 4.0 per sample
  tissue 1: every patient has a sample here
  tissue 2: 24 patient(s) have no sample here, and get a row of per-gene means padded in
  the counts look usable

Those 24 patients are kept, and the full model is given a made-up profile for the tissue they lack: the rounded per-gene mean of that tissue's real samples, linked to nothing in that tissue's network. The guide's full-model section says what such a row does and does not contribute to. The number is worth reading, because it is the share of the cohort the model will be working on that was made up rather than measured.

docs.title: preffect train
docs.text:
Fits a model to the training counts and writes it to one file.

preffect train --train my_study/train --validation my_study/validation \
               --out model.pt --epochs 100 --seed 0 --threads 16

The data

Option What it does Default --train folder of training counts required --validation folder of validation counts, used to report a loss on samples the model is not fitted to none --out the file to write the model to; its folder is created if missing, and the path is checked for writability before any work starts required --tissues how many tissue files each folder holds 1 --genes keep only this many of the most variable genes, chosen on the training data and applied to the validation data by name all genes

The model

Option What it does Default --kind simple uses counts alone; single adds one sample-sample network; full uses several matched tissues per patient simple --likelihood which count distribution the model fits: NB, the negative binomial, or ZINB, which adds a separate probability that a count is zero for a reason unrelated to expression level; see below NB --latent-dim the size of the summary the model learns for each sample 20 --hidden-dim the width of the hidden layers between the counts and that summary 50

The fitting

Option What it does Default --epochs how many passes over the training data; --patience below says how many is enough, and for what 100 --batch-size how many samples go through the model per step 100 --learning-rate how far the optimiser moves per step 0.001 --patience stop early once the loss has not improved for this many epochs; the model kept is the best epoch's never stop early --min-delta how much the loss must fall to count as improving, for --patience 0 --stop-on what --patience watches: loss, or imputation, the error on the entries --hide hid; see below loss --hide hide this fraction of the training entries at random, score the model against the full counts, and report the error on the hidden entries at the end; the sample totals the model scales by are corrected for what the hiding took away (see below); needed for --stop-on imputation nothing hidden --edge-balance how the single and full models score the pairs of samples that are not linked: balanced gives the linked pairs the same total weight as the absent ones, none scores every pair equally; see below balanced

Running it

Option What it does Default --seed fixes the random starting point, so the same command gives the same model twice unseeded --deterministic repeatable bit for bit on a GPU as well as on the CPU; needs --seed off --threads compute threads 4 --device cpu, cuda, or a particular card such as cuda:0 cpu

Starting from a model already fitted

Option What it does Default --from-model a saved model to start from instead of from scratch; it must have the same genes and the same shape, and the command says which differs if not none --freeze hold part of the model still while the rest trains, for example --freeze encoder; may be given more than once; only with --from-model nothing frozen

Output on the vignette data, with --patience 5:

fitting a simple model: 200 genes, 36,090 parameters, 80 epochs
finished after 8 epoch(s)
  training loss   1456.05 -> 947.48
  validation loss 1119.80
  stopped early, best epoch was 3
wrote model.pt

Validation close to training means the model is not simply memorising. A validation loss far above the training loss means it is, and the vignette's toy of 120 samples gets there within a few epochs, which is why it runs with --patience.

docs.title: Worth knowing
docs.text:
Set --seed if you want the same model twice. Without it the same command gives a different model each time. On a GPU, add --deterministic as well. Without it two runs of a graph model from the same seed differ at the fourth decimal place, because one of its operations adds numbers in whichever order the card finishes them; with it the two runs match bit for bit, measured on an A100. The simple model matches on a GPU either way. Deterministic kernels can be slower, which has not been measured, so it is off unless asked for.

--likelihood ZINB is for counts that have more zeros than the negative binomial can account for. The negative binomial already produces plenty of zeros on its own when a gene is lowly expressed, so a high proportion of them is not by itself a reason to change. The zero-inflated form adds a separate probability that a count is zero for a reason unrelated to expression level, such as the transcript never being captured, and it costs one more parameter per gene and sample along with the layer that produces it.

The PREFFECT paper found little evidence that fRNA-seq needs it, which is why NB is the default. To ask the question of your own counts rather than inheriting that answer, fit both distributions to them and compare: Choosing a distribution. The choice is saved with the model, so apply rebuilds the distribution the model was fitted with and does not need telling again.

Set --threads to suit the size of your data. PyTorch otherwise starts one compute thread per core, which on a large shared machine can be over a hundred, and coordinating them costs more than the arithmetic. The default of 4 suits a small example. Measured on 528 samples by 18,790 genes, in seconds per epoch: 1 thread 3.9, 4 threads 2.1, 8 threads 1.3, 16 threads 1.2, 32 threads 1.6. On small data one thread wins.

--validation is optional, and leaving it out is honest. A cohort too small to split should not use a copy of the training data as its validation set; without one, no validation loss is computed and none is reported.

--genes chooses once, on the training data. The validation set gets the same genes, matched by name, never re-chosen. The saved model records the names, and apply matches on them.

--patience stops a run that has stopped improving, and it stops early. It watches the validation loss, or the training loss when there is no --validation, and stops once that has not fallen by at least --min-delta for --patience epochs in a row; the model written is the best epoch's, not the last. On a cohort of 220 samples at the default learning rate, with a fifth of the samples held out, the validation loss is lowest at about epoch 450 and within five per cent of that until 4,000, so any patience stops at 240 to 830 epochs. That is the right place to stop if the model is for samples it has not seen. It is ten times too soon if the model is for the cohort it was fitted on: imputation of that cohort's hidden entries is 1.5 times worse at epoch 300 than at 3,000 and is still falling at 16,000, and the loss that --patience watches cannot see it. Clustering recovery of subtype from the latent is at its level by epoch 500 to 750 whichever you do, and past 7,000 the latent of unseen samples gets worse. At this learning rate, 3,000 to 5,000 epochs serves the loss and the latent within a few per cent and in-cohort imputation within about a tenth, and 16,000 is harmful for anything applied to new samples. A rule that watches imputation of the hidden entries instead, which lands near that range on its own, is below.

--stop-on imputation stops where imputation of the fitted cohort settles. With --hide 0.2 a fifth of the training entries are hidden from the model at random, and after every epoch the model's error on those entries is measured, --patience then counts epochs without that error falling, and the model written is the best epoch's by that measure. On a real cohort, a patience of 500 to 2,000 epochs stops at 2,000 to 4,000 and keeps a model within four to six per cent of the best imputation, where the loss rule keeps one from epoch 300 with 1.7 times the error. Two things to know. The objective scores the model against the full counts, hidden entries included, so this measures how far the fit of the cohort has gone, not how the model generalises to samples it has not seen; for that, stop on the loss with --validation. And measuring it costs one extra pass over the training data per epoch, about 70 per cent more time an epoch on a GPU; the random stream is restored afterwards, so the run is the same run as without the rule, stopped sooner or later. Run live on that cohort, the rule stopped at 2,100 to 6,400 epochs on its own and kept a model ten per cent better at imputation than a fixed 4,000-epoch run, with the latent space level or better, at 1.7 times the time. --min-delta applies to whichever quantity is watched, in its own units. With the default of zero the imputation rule waits until the error stops falling at all; on data where it keeps creeping down (synthetic data can fall two per cent over 4,000 epochs, so the rule runs to its cap) set --min-delta to the smallest improvement worth waiting for, about one per cent of the error: 0.005 on an error near 0.5, 0.01 on one near 1.

--hide corrects the sample totals for what it hid. A sample's library size is its total count, and the model multiplies everything it predicts for that sample by it. Hiding a fifth of the entries takes about a fifth off that total, while the counts the model is scored against keep the originals, so without a correction every predicted count is short by the hidden fraction and no amount of training recovers it: the composition sums to one across genes, so the library alone sets the scale. The correction is each sample's gene count divided by the number of its entries the model was shown, which reads how many entries were hidden and never which values. It applies only to --hide, which hides entries at random; nothing else about a run changes, and a run without --hide is unaffected.

--edge-balance decides how the graph models score the pairs of samples that are not linked. A sample-sample network links each sample to a few others out of hundreds, so 92 to 99.8 per cent of the pairs are not edges, and scoring every pair equally, which none does, leaves the network half of the model with nothing to learn: it settles on predicting no edge anywhere, and the loss cannot show it because that is exactly the prediction the loss rewards. balanced, the default, gives the linked pairs the same total weight as the absent ones. On synthetic data with a known network the predicted network then ranks the true edges as well as a predictor that knows the sample groups, with clustering, imputation and the expression terms unchanged; on the real cohorts tried so far it has not recovered a usable network, though nothing measured is worse under it. So do not expect a usable network out of a graph model without checking the ranking with network_recovery on your own data.

Two further things to know. Under balanced a probability above one half is not an edge call: equal weight moves the point where the model is undecided, so most pairs come out above a half and the useful output is the ranking, which is how the guide's network_recovery scores it. And none is there for repeating a result produced with the unweighted term.

--batch-size matters more for the graph models. A graph model can only attend to network edges between samples that are in the same batch, so a batch much smaller than the cohort hides most of the network from it. For single and full, consider a batch size equal to the number of samples. How much this costs has not been measured.

A part that does not exist cannot be frozen. --freeze encodr is refused, with the parts that do exist listed, rather than freezing nothing while appearing to.

docs.title: preffect apply
docs.text:
Runs a saved model over counts and writes the cleaned result.

preffect apply --model model.pt --data my_study/new --out cleaned.h5ad
Option What it does Default --model the file train wrote required --data folder of counts to apply it to required --out the .h5ad file to write; checked for writability before the model is loaded required --tissues how many tissue files the data folder holds; only consulted if the model did not record its own count, and a model saved by this version always does 1 --threads compute threads, as for train 4 --device cpu, cuda, or a particular card such as cuda:0, as for train cpu

Output on the vignette's held-out split:

loaded a simple model written by PREFFECT 0.2.0.dev0, applying on cpu
matched 200 genes to the ones the model was fitted on
wrote cleaned.h5ad: 40 samples, 200 genes

The result carries the cleaned counts in X, the predicted proportions in layers['composition'], and the latent summary of each sample in obsm['latent'].

Genes are matched by name, so the columns of the file you apply to need not be in the order you trained on. A gene the model was fitted on and the file lacks stops the command and says which, rather than shifting everything along by one.

apply will run over any counts, including the ones the model was trained on. The only honest held-out result comes from data that was in neither --train nor --validation.

docs.title: preffect gui
docs.text:
Opens the graphical interface in your browser: prepare and look at a folder of counts, apply a saved model, read how the fit went, and look at the figures, a page at a time. It answers on this machine only, to localhost, and sends nothing anywhere; from a laptop, forward the port over SSH.

preffect gui
Option What it does Default --port the local port to serve on 8501

It needs the gui extra, and says so if that is missing.

docs.title: preffect example-data
docs.text:
Writes a small simulated cohort, so the commands above can be tried before any real data is to hand, and so the worked example runs from a tool install, which has no copy of the source.

preffect example-data --out example_data
Option What it does Default --out the folder to write under example_data --seed seed for the simulation; the same seed writes the same files 0 --unmatched the share of patients whose second tissue is left out of the full model's data, so there is something to pad; at least 0 and below 1 0

It writes three things, each as three splits with no sample in common: simple/ for the simple model; single/, the same counts plus a sample-sample network with real edges in it; and full/, two tissues per patient under different names with the correspondence table the full model needs. 200 genes, three groups of samples that each raise a different block of genes, negative binomial counts. It checks that no two splits share a sample or are the same file before it reports success, and refuses to write otherwise. At --unmatched 0 it draws no random numbers for the gaps, so the files are the same whether the option exists or not.

Three further things are true of what it writes, and each exists so an example can show something a real cohort shows. The genes are drawn once per cohort, so a cohort's three splits are the same genes and a model fitted on one can be applied to another. Batch B's own genes are raised by a factor of 1.3, a fifth of them picked at random and listed in the file under uns['batch_shifted_genes'], which is a nuisance for the correction variables to take out and is deliberately weaker than the groups. Every file carries the count each entry was drawn from, in layers['true_expected_counts'], so a filled-in entry can be scored against the signal rather than against one noisy draw of it.

docs.title: When it refuses
docs.text:
The message names what was asked for and what to do instead. A few you may meet:

It says It means no such folder the path given to --train, --validation or --data does not exist no files matching '*tau_<n>.h5ad' the folder exists but holds no count file named the way PREFFECT expects gene name(s) appear more than once gene names are the key everything matches on, and some repeat; it lists them, worst first the validation data is the training data printed by check, not a refusal: your two splits hold the same samples a network with NO edges between samples the file carries a sample-sample network with nothing in it; use --kind simple cannot write --out the output path was checked before any work and cannot be written --freeze only makes sense with --from-model there is nothing to hold still in a model that has not been fitted count(s) are not whole numbers, at ... from prepare: the counts table holds normalised or log-transformed values; it names the entries links every sample to every other --neighbours is one short of the sample count or more, which says nothing about which samples resemble which already in that folder prepare and network refuse to write over a file; give another --out or pass --overwrite already carries a sample-sample network network will not rebuild a real one unless --replace says so

If a message tells you only that something is wrong and not what to do about it, that is a defect in the message, and worth reporting.

docs.title: What the command line does not reach
docs.text: Imputation scored against a genuine held-out set, clustering the latent summary, and figures are done from Python. Using it covers them.

docs.title: Installing
docs.text: PREFFECT needs Python 3.11 or newer. There is no release on the Python Package Index; it installs from GitHub.

docs.title: One command, if you only want to run it
docs.text:
uv tool install git+https://github.com/hallettmiket/preffect

That builds PREFFECT in an environment of its own and puts a preffect command on your path. There is no copy of the source to keep and nothing to activate. It needs uv.

The parts used for figures and for grouping samples are optional, because fitting a model does not need a plotting stack. Ask for them by name:

uv tool install "preffect[viz] @ git+https://github.com/hallettmiket/preffect"

Later, uv tool upgrade preffect moves you to a newer version and uv tool uninstall preffect removes it.

docs.title: On a machine without a GPU
docs.text:
Ask for PyTorch 2.6 from PyTorch's CPU index at the same time:

uv tool install "preffect @ git+https://github.com/hallettmiket/preffect" \
    --with "torch==2.6.*" --index https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cpu

Two reasons. The default download of PyTorch carries several gigabytes of GPU libraries a machine without a GPU cannot use; the CPU build is a few hundred megabytes. And from release 2.7 on, PyTorch's CPU kernels are slower, dropout most of all, by about a quarter of a training step on this model; 2.6 is the package's floor, so nothing is lost by staying on it. The measurements are on the speed page. With pip, install torch first and PREFFECT second: pip install "torch==2.6.*" --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cpu.

docs.title: A copy of the source, if you want to change it
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/hallettmiket/preffect.git
cd preffect
bash scripts/install.sh

That makes an isolated environment in .venv, installs PREFFECT and everything optional into it, and then checks its own work: that the package imports, that the preffect command runs, and that the fast tests pass. If any of those fail it says so rather than reporting success. Add --minimal for the models, training and inference alone.

It uses uv when uv is installed, because uv is several times faster, and falls back to the standard library's venv and pip when it is not. It will not download and run an installer from the internet to get uv.

This route leaves the command at .venv/bin/preffect rather than on your path, which is deliberate: the copy you are editing cannot then be confused with one installed somewhere else.

docs.title: Installing it yourself instead
docs.text:
python -m venv .venv
.venv/bin/pip install -e .

That gives you the models, training and inference. Three extras add the rest:

.venv/bin/pip install -e '.[graph]'    # the single and full models
.venv/bin/pip install -e '.[cluster]'  # grouping samples, scoring the grouping
.venv/bin/pip install -e '.[viz]'      # the above, plus figures

docs.title: Check it worked
docs.text:
preffect --version

If that prints something unexpected, run it as python -P -m preffect --version. Python puts the current folder at the front of the import path, so a folder named preffect sitting next to where you are standing wins over the one you installed. -P turns that off. This is not hypothetical: it is how the install script's own check first failed.

The rest of this page writes the command as preffect. If you took a copy of the source instead, write .venv/bin/preffect everywhere it appears.

docs.title: What your data has to look like
docs.text:
One folder per split, each containing an .h5ad file, which is the AnnData format:

my_study/
    train/
        counts.h5ad
    validation/        # optional
        counts.h5ad

Inside that file:

  • X is the counts: rows are samples, columns are genes. Whole numbers. Not normalised, not log-transformed. PREFFECT models counts, so a log-transformed matrix will not fit and the check below will say so.
  • var_names are the gene names, and they have to be unique. They are the key everything matches on.
  • obs may carry anything you want to use later: a batch, a subtype.
  • obsm['sample_sample_adj'] is the sample-sample network, if you have one. Only the single and full models use it.

docs.title: Building that file from the tables you have
docs.text:
Almost nobody's counts arrive in that shape. preffect prepare builds it from the two tables a study does have: the counts, and a row per sample saying what is known about it.

Say your counts are in counts.csv, one row per sample, with the sample names in the first column and the gene names in the first row:

,GENE_0000,GENE_0001,GENE_0002
BX_000,74,66,58
BX_001,90,53,52

The first cell may be empty, as it is here, or hold a heading of its own.

and samples.csv has a row per sample, again with the names in the first column:

sample,subtype,batch,patient
BX_000,basal,A,PT_000
BX_001,basal,B,PT_001

Then one command writes the file:

preffect prepare \
    --counts counts.csv \
    --samples samples.csv \
    --out my_study/train \
    --neighbours 10 \
    --label subtype

tissue 1: 60 samples and 400 genes from counts.csv, read as samples-by-genes
  3 annotation(s) per sample from samples.csv
  tissue 1: 60 samples, 371 edge(s), 12.4 per sample (fewest 10, middle 11, most 19); no isolated samples
  tissue 1: 100.0% of edges join two samples with the same subtype, against 32.2% if the edges ignored it
wrote my_study/train/counts.tau_1.h5ad
check it with: preffect check --train my_study/train

Four things in that command are worth knowing about.

--counts-are genes-by-samples reads a counts table written the other way round, one row per gene, which is how many pipelines write one. Without it the table is read as one row per sample, and a table the wrong way round is refused rather than transposed on a guess.

--neighbours 10 builds the sample-sample network the single and full models need, by linking each sample to the ten others whose counts look most like its own. Leave it out and no network is written, which is right for the simple model. Ten is the number this project measured; the command line page says where it comes from. If your files already exist and only the network is missing, preffect network adds one to them without this command.

--label subtype says whether the network found anything. It compares the share of links joining two samples with the same subtype against the share that would do so if the links ignored subtype entirely. The second line above is a network that found real structure. Two numbers close together mean it found none, and a graph model over that network will cost ten times the parameters of the simple model for nothing.

It refuses rather than repairs. Counts that are not whole numbers, a negative count, a repeated gene name, a sample table describing different samples from the counts: each stops the command with a sentence naming the entries at fault.

For the full model, give --counts and --samples once per tissue and name the column that says which patient each sample came from. That builds the correspondence table the full model needs, and a patient with no sample in some tissue is kept with a gap recorded rather than dropped.

docs.title: Always run the check first
docs.text:
preffect check --train my_study/train --validation my_study/validation

This reads the data, reports what it found, and refuses if something would stop a run. It takes seconds and it is the single most useful command here, because the problems it finds are ones that otherwise show up as a confusing result rather than as an error.

On real data it has caught, among other things, twenty-one genes all sharing one name, a validation set that was a byte-for-byte copy of the training set, and a sample-sample network with no edges in it.

Output on a healthy dataset:

training: 1 tissue(s) from my_study/train
  tissue 1: 528 samples, 18790 genes, a network with 105 edge(s), 1.0 per sample
  the counts look usable
validation: 61 samples from my_study/validation
  tissue 1: 0 of 528 training samples reappear in validation

docs.title: Fitting a model
docs.text:
preffect train \
    --train my_study/train \
    --validation my_study/validation \
    --out model.pt \
    --epochs 100 \
    --seed 0 \
    --threads 16

Two of those are worth knowing about.

--seed makes the run repeatable. Without it the same command gives a different model each time.

--threads matters more than you would expect. PyTorch otherwise starts one compute thread per core, which on a large shared machine can be over a hundred, and coordinating them costs more than the arithmetic. The right number depends on the size of the data. Measured on 528 samples by 18,790 genes, seconds per epoch:

threads 1 4 8 16 32 seconds per epoch 3.9 2.1 1.3 1.2 1.6

On small data the ordering reverses and one thread wins. The default of 4 suits a small test rather than a real cohort.

docs.title: Applying it
docs.text:
preffect apply \
    --model model.pt \
    --data my_study/train \
    --out cleaned.h5ad

The result carries the cleaned counts in X, the predicted proportions in layers['composition'], and the latent summary in obsm['latent'].

Genes are matched to the ones the model was fitted on by name, so the column order of the file you apply to does not have to match the one you trained on. If a gene is missing, it says so rather than quietly shifting everything along by one.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: The command line is every option of the three commands above, with what each is for and when to change it. Using it covers the parts the command line does not reach: imputation with a held-out set, clustering, and figures.

docs.title: The graphical interface
docs.text:
A page in your browser for the part of the work you want to look at: turning your two tables into the file PREFFECT reads, whether that folder of counts can be fitted and what it holds, how the fit that produced a saved model went, and the figures that say whether to believe it. It reads like a report. The pages sit under six headings in the sidebar, in the order the work is done, and you move through them a page at a time. Past the figures it will look up a single gene or a single sample, ask whether the model can fill in a count it was not shown, and put two saved models side by side on the same counts.

preffect gui

That starts a local server and opens the page. It needs the gui extra: pip install "preffect[gui]", or uv tool install "preffect[gui] @ git+https://github.com/hallettmiket/preffect". preffect gui says so if it is missing.

It answers on this machine only and sends nothing anywhere. The page is served to localhost and to nothing else, so nobody on the network can open it, and Streamlit's own usage reporting, which the library it is built on turns on by default, is turned off by the command that starts it. Press Ctrl+C in the terminal to stop it. --port changes the port if 8501 is taken.

If PREFFECT runs on a server and you are at a laptop, forward the port over SSH and open the same address in your own browser:

ssh -L 8501:localhost:8501 your-server    # then preffect gui on the server

docs.title: How it is laid out
docs.text:
The sidebar lists the pages under six headings, top to bottom in the order the work is done. Each title is the question the page answers, and clicking it opens that page and nothing else. A page is listed only once what it needs is open, so before a run is open you see four pages, and the rest appear when a model has been applied. Under the list, three lines say what is open, on every page: the folder of counts, the model, and the second model if there is one. Every page opens by saying what it is for, before any number or picture. Each page has an address of its own, so a figure page can be bookmarked and returned to.

Heading Pages Needs Start Start here nothing Your data Prepare the input file; Can this be fitted?; What does the data look like? a folder of counts, for the last two The fit How did the fit go? a run Does the fit hold? one page per figure, six in all a run Ask the model What did it make of one gene or sample?; Can it fill in hidden counts? a run Compare How do two models compare? a second model, opened on the same counts

docs.title: Start here
docs.text:
The landing page. It says in one sentence what the interface is for and that fitting itself happens on the command line, then says whether a run is open, and then asks for what it needs: the folder of counts and how many tissue files are in it, the model preffect train wrote and the device to run it on, and, optionally, a second model to compare. A folded section at the bottom walks the four steps for a first visit, and stays folded after that.

Nothing to open yet? Press Try it on the example data and the interface writes the simulated example cohort under the system's temporary folder, fits the worked example's two models on it, a plain one and a zero-inflated one, with the worked example's own settings, fills in the paths it made and opens both. It takes about ten seconds. It is the one fit the interface makes: the cohort is small and simulated, and the fit goes through the same preffect train the worked example runs. Every page then has something behind it, and the comparison page has two different models to put side by side. Nothing is filled in until you press it, because a path that only exists on one machine is not a default this package will ship.

A run is a saved model and the counts you want to apply it to. Give both and press Open the run. Applying the model takes a moment and then happens once: moving between pages after that does not refit or reapply anything, and the line at the top of the page says what is open. The three pages under Your data need only the folder, so you can prepare, check and look at a cohort before you have fitted anything.

Name a second model and press Open the comparison and it is applied to the same counts, which adds the Compare heading. Opening a different first run drops the second, because two models over two different sets of counts is not a comparison and nothing on the page would say so.

docs.title: Prepare the input file
docs.text:
Writes the file everything else here reads, from the two tables you are likely to have: a counts table with a count for every sample and gene, and a sample table saying what is known about each sample. It is preffect prepare with the steps laid out, and it is where to start if PREFFECT has never seen your cohort.

Upload the two tables, or type their paths, which is usually right when PREFFECT runs on a server you reached over an SSH tunnel and the files are already there. Say which way round the counts are written: one row per sample is assumed, and one row per gene, which is how many pipelines write one, is flipped as it is read. The page then says how many samples and genes it found and what columns the sample table has, so a table read the wrong way round is obvious before anything is built.

Two things are optional:

  • A sample-sample network, which only the single and full models use. A slider sets how many samples each one links to, and the summary underneath redraws as it moves: edges, links per sample, and samples left with none. Name a column of your sample table and it also gives the share of links joining two samples with that same label against the share that would join by chance. Two shares close together mean the network carries no biology.
  • The table saying which sample is which patient, which the full model needs and which appears once you ask for two tissues or more. Choose the column naming the patient and the page says how many patients have a sample in each tissue and how many have none.

Name a folder, press the button, and one file per tissue is written. Nothing already in the folder is written over: a name that is taken is refused, with the path it would have replaced. Every count is checked before anything is written and a problem names the entries at fault. The page finishes by running the same check the next page runs, so you end on the sentence that says whether what you made can be fitted.

docs.title: Can this be fitted?
docs.text: What preffect check reports, and it needs no model. It says how many samples and genes each tissue file holds, whether there is a sample-sample network and how many links it has, and, if something would stop a run, the sentence the run would have refused with. It is a pass or a fail. Run it on a new folder before you spend hours fitting anything.

docs.title: What does the data look like?
docs.text:
What the folder holds, read without a model, for the decisions that come before a fit. For each tissue file:

  • how many samples and genes there are, and how much of the matrix is zero, which is what decides whether to ask preffect train for the zero-inflated distribution, --likelihood ZINB: a matrix that is largely zeros is where it earns its extra parameter, and one that is not usually does not need it;
  • the sample table's columns, with how many distinct values each takes, how many are missing and a few examples, which is where a batch to correct for or a label to colour the latent summary by comes from;
  • whether the file carries a sample-sample network, and with how many links, which only the graph models use;
  • how deeply each sample was sequenced, as a histogram of each sample's total count. A bar far to the right of the rest is a sample sequenced far more deeply than the others and one far to the left is a failed library; either pulls a fit towards itself, and this is the moment to drop it, before any model has been pulled by it.

The page before this one says whether the folder can be fitted at all; this one says what you would be fitting.

docs.title: How did the fit go?
docs.text:
Describes the fit itself, and it is the page to read first once a run is open. It is there so that nobody reads a figure without first knowing whether the model behind it had finished moving. It shows, in this order:

  • what was fitted: the kind of model, the count distribution it used, how many samples and genes were matched, and how many tissue files it holds
  • the settings that change what the numbers mean: whether the library size was read from the counts or inferred by the model, the batch size and the learning rate
  • how the fit went: how many epochs it ran out of how many were asked for, whether it stopped early, which epoch's weights were saved, how long the fitting took, and one sentence saying how the run ended
  • the loss curve: the mean loss per batch at every epoch, with the validation curve on the same axes where there was a validation split
  • a button to download the cleaned counts as an .h5ad file, the same file preffect apply writes

A model saved by an older version of PREFFECT says so. The loss curve, the epoch count and the timing come from a record preffect train now writes into the model file. A file written before that was kept is still a perfectly good model: the page says it was saved before its history was kept, and everything that does not need the history is shown as usual. Refit if you want the curve.

docs.title: Does the fit hold?
docs.text:
Each figure gets a page of its own, titled with the question it answers, and each page opens by saying what the picture shows, what a good one looks like, what a bad one looks like and what to do about it. They are written for someone who has not read the code, and they come in order from the simplest check of the fit to the latent summary:

Page What is drawn Does it track sequencing depth? each sample's observed total count beside the total the model inferred Does it reproduce the counts? for the most variable genes, the count the model fitted against the count observed, sample by sample Did it remove the batch effect? each gene's average in one batch against its average in another, in the data and in the model's view of it Is the noise per gene believable? gene averages, fitted dispersion, library sizes, and the dispersion against the average Does it get the zeros right? how often each gene is zero against the zero-inflated model's probability of a zero Do similar samples group together? the model's summary of each sample squeezed to two dimensions, coloured by a column of your sample table

Two of these need something the model may not have. Did it remove the batch effect? needs a column of your sample table holding one label per sample, such as the run or the site it came from, and you choose which column on the page. Does it get the zeros right? needs the zero-inflated distribution, which is preffect train --likelihood ZINB. Where what is needed is missing, the page still opens with its description and says in a sentence what is missing and what to refit with, rather than drawing something empty.

Every figure here is one of preffect.plots' figures, drawn by the same call a script would make, so anything seen here can be reproduced and put in a paper. The loss curve on the fit page is the one exception, and it is drawn from what the training run recorded.

docs.title: What did it make of one gene or sample?
docs.text:
Answers a question about one gene or one sample, where every page before it describes the whole cohort at once. Pick a gene and it shows the count the model fitted in each sample against the count observed, how closely the two move together across the cohort, how variable the model thinks the gene is, and how often it is zero. Pick a sample and it gives one number saying how well the model accounts for that sample, and shows where that number sits among the rest.

The measure for a sample is the mean log probability per gene of that sample's observed counts under the distribution the model fitted for it. Larger is better and every value is negative, because these are probabilities of a particular count. It is taken per gene rather than summed over genes so that it does not grow with the size of the panel.

The part worth your time is the list at the bottom, which is the cohort ordered worst fit first. A sample at the top of it is usually a failed library, a mislabelled sample, or a sample of a different tissue from the rest, and it is worth looking at before it goes into anything downstream.

docs.title: Can it fill in hidden counts?
docs.text:
Asks whether the model can fill in a count it was not shown. It hides a fraction of the entries of the counts you loaded, chosen by a slider and a seed, runs the model on what is left, and compares what it predicted at the hidden entries against what was really there. This is what preffect train --hide reports at the end of a run, asked of a model that is already fitted.

The number is the average relative distance from the observed count, so 0.5 means the typical filled-in entry is out by half of the count that was there, and smaller is better. It comes with how many entries it was scored over and how many were left out, because a relative error cannot be computed where the true value is zero.

Read it as a statement about this cohort, not about new samples. The model has already seen every sample here. Filling a gap for a patient it has never met is a harder question, and it needs a held-out folder.

Where the file carries layers['true_expected_counts'], which only simulated data can have, the page also scores against that, which is the better comparison: an observed count is one draw from a distribution, so part of the distance from it is noise nothing could have predicted. On the worked example the same model is out by about 65 per cent of the observed count and about 12 per cent of the count it was drawn from. Ordinary counts carry no such layer, and PREFFECT will not invent one.

docs.title: How do two models compare?
docs.text:
Appears once a second model has been opened on the same counts, so that the difference you see is the model and not the data. It has three parts: what each run recorded about itself, side by side; any figure page drawn under both models on one set of axes; and a table of three numbers you might decide on, worked out when you ask because clustering costs a minute on a real cohort. Those three are the median correlation between fitted and observed across genes, the latent clustering scored against a column of your sample table, and the imputation error, which reuses the fraction and seed the page above it used.

The last column of the table says which run is better on each measure, and reads neither where the two differ by less than a threshold set for that table: 0.01 for a correlation, 0.05 for the adjusted Rand index, and five per cent for the imputation error.

Those thresholds stop a tiny difference being read as a result. They are not a measurement of the noise. This page compares two particular fits, not two methods: fitting either model again from a different seed gives a different answer. Treat a small difference here as nothing at all.

docs.title: What it does not do
docs.text:
It does not fit a model, apart from the example on the landing page, which is seconds on simulated data and goes through preffect train itself. Training a real cohort is hours, and belongs on the command line where it can be left running and logged. The interface reads what preffect train wrote. That is why the count distribution is shown here and chosen there, with preffect train --likelihood: a zero-inflated model and a plain one of the same kind look alike on these pages and predict different counts, so the page owes you the answer even though it cannot change it. The same holds for everything else on the fit page: it reports the settings a run used and changes none of them.

It does not score anything on samples it has not seen. The imputation page hides entries of the counts you loaded and scores the model on putting them back, which is a statement about this cohort and not about new patients. The comparison page scores the latent clustering against one column you choose. Anything past those two, a held-out folder or a decision about what to compare against, is Using it from Python.

docs.title: If something is wrong
docs.text: A folder that cannot be read, counts that would stop a run, or a device the machine lacks shows as a sentence on the page, the same sentence the command line prints. A figure that cannot be drawn from this particular model says so on its own page, in the sentence preffect.plots refuses with. If the latent figure says it needs the viz extra, the gui extra includes it, so that is an environment assembled by hand; install it.

docs.title: Using it
docs.text: The command line covers fitting and applying. This page covers the rest, from Python.

docs.title: Fitting from Python
docs.text:
from pathlib import Path

import torch

from preffect.config import (
    DataConfig, LossWeights, ModelConfig, PreffectConfig,
    RuntimeConfig, TrainConfig,
)
from preffect.data.checks import check_tissues
from preffect.data.loading import load_tissues
from preffect.data.tensors import to_tensors
from preffect.model import SimpleModel
from preffect.training import configure_runtime, train

tissues = load_tissues(Path("my_study/train"), n_tissues=1)
check_tissues(tissues, split="training")      # raises if something is wrong
data = to_tensors(tissues[0], correction_variables=())

config = PreffectConfig(
    data=DataConfig(train_path=Path("my_study/train")),
    model=ModelConfig(latent_dim=20, hidden_dim=256),
    loss=LossWeights(),
    train=TrainConfig(epochs=100, batch_size=64, learning_rate=1e-3),
    runtime=RuntimeConfig(seed=0, num_threads=16),
)

configure_runtime(config)                      # before building the model
model = SimpleModel(tissues[0].n_vars, config.model)
history = train(model, data, config)

configure_runtime sets the seed and the thread count, and it has to run before the model is built. Weights are initialised during construction, so seeding afterwards leaves the initialisation unseeded and the run unrepeatable. train calls it too, so a run that only uses train is covered.

docs.title: The full model, and patients who are missing a tissue
docs.text:
The full model reads several profiles from the same patient and predicts the first one. It needs to know which row of one file is which row of another, and the files deliberately do not share sample names, so the correspondence is written down in a table under obsm['sample_association'] with one column per tissue. read_split finds it, reorders every tissue by it, and hands back tissues whose row i is the same patient throughout.

A patient can be missing a tissue, and is kept rather than refused. A cohort where some patients have no matched normal is the ordinary case. Their cell in the table is empty, and PREFFECT gives that tissue a row of its own for them, called a padded row here:

  • its counts are the rounded per-gene mean of that tissue's real samples;
  • every annotation is missing;
  • it has no links in that tissue's sample-sample network, so it attends to nothing and nothing attends to it.

What a padded row contributes to, and what it does not. It is left out of the expression reconstruction term and both library-size terms, which are the three terms that read the counts. It is kept in the latent and network terms, so it is encoded and it takes part in the attention.

Two consequences worth knowing before you fit:

  • Nothing is ever hidden in a padded row. Its counts are a mean this package invented, so recovering one would measure nothing. A mask that hides an entry in a padded row is refused by name rather than quietly worked around.
  • Padding and correction variables cannot be combined. A padded row has no annotations, so it has no batch and no stage, and a correction variable with a missing value is refused. Fill the annotations in yourself, drop the incomplete patients, or leave the correction variables out.

What comes out leaves them behind. infer and preffect apply return results for the real rows of the predicted tissue only, and report how many padded rows they dropped, in n_padded_rows_dropped and in uns["padded_rows_dropped"] of the file apply writes.

preffect check tells you how many there are before you fit anything, one line per tissue, which is the share of the cohort that will be made up rather than measured. The command line page shows the output.

To drop the incomplete patients instead, ask the alignment to refuse them and act on what it names:

from preffect.data.tissues import align_tissues, unmatched_counts

print(unmatched_counts(tissues))        # {'tau_1': 0, 'tau_2': 24}
alignment = align_tissues(tissues, unmatched="refuse")   # raises if any are missing

docs.title: Imputation
docs.text:
To find out how well it fills gaps, hide some entries, fit on what is left, and score only the hidden ones.

import numpy as np

from preffect.data.masking import apply_mask, mcar_mask
from preffect.data.tensors import TensorData
from preffect.inference import imputation_error, infer

truth = torch.from_numpy(counts)
mask = mcar_mask(n_samples, n_genes, fraction=0.2, rng=np.random.default_rng(0))
shown = torch.from_numpy(apply_mask(counts, mask))

model_data = TensorData(inputs=shown, targets=truth, mask=mask)
train(model, model_data, config)

result = infer(model, model_data)
scores = imputation_error(
    result.expected_counts, truth,
    hidden=torch.from_numpy(mask.hidden), kind="mean_relative",
)
print(scores["hidden"], scores["visible"])

To stop training where that error settles rather than where the loss does, which is ten times sooner, ask for it in the settings and hide entries as above: TrainConfig(early_stopping_patience=1000, stop_on="imputation"). The command line page says what the two rules measure and when each is the right one.

Truth is an argument, with no default
