imputation_error will not invent something to compare against. Pass the true values, or the observed counts at the hidden entries, and it scores against those.

The library size is corrected for what the hiding took away. A sample's library size is its total count, and the model multiplies everything it predicts for that sample by it. Read off the counts the model was shown, that total is short by the hidden fraction, while the targets keep the originals, so every predicted count would be short by the same fraction and nothing in the model could make it up: the composition sums to one across genes, so the library alone sets the scale. Passing a mask to TensorData, as above, is all it takes. The correction is the number of genes divided by the number of that sample's entries the model was shown, and it travels with the data through training, mini-batching and inference.

The correction reads how many entries were hidden and never which values. A sample's true total together with its visible entries would give the sum of its hidden ones exactly, so a library taken from the targets would hand the model the answer it is being scored on. It is also available for missing completely at random only, which is the one scheme mcar_mask writes; a scheme that hid entries according to their values would make the estimate biased rather than unavailable, and is refused by name.

Scoring the visible entries too is worth doing. Doing well on entries the model was shown is not imputation, and if the two numbers are similar the model may be reproducing its input rather than generalising.

Relative error leaves out entries whose true value is zero, and reports how many it left out. Dividing by zero makes an average meaningless, and counts are 10 to 55 per cent zeros.

docs.title: Scoring a predicted network
docs.text:
The single and full models reconstruct the sample-sample network from a latent space of their own, and the loss cannot say whether they are getting it right: on a network one per cent dense, a model that predicts no edge anywhere scores well on an unweighted cross-entropy. Score the edges instead.

from preffect.inference import network_recovery

model.eval()
with torch.no_grad():
    output = model(data.inputs, data.corrections, data.edge_index)
    predicted = model.network_decoder(output.network_latent_mean, data.corrections)

scores = network_recovery(predicted, data.adjacency_matrix())
print(scores)
# precision 0.021, recall 1.000, F1 0.041 at one half (111259 pairs predicted,
# 2355 edges among 179700 pairs); average precision 0.039 against 0.013 for a
# flat prediction

That output is a single model after 200 epochs on a synthetic cohort with a known network: the ranking is three times better than chance, and the threshold of one half calls far too many pairs, which is the kind of thing the loss alone would never have shown.

Both inputs are square over the same samples and are read as symmetric: each pair is counted once and the diagonal is ignored. An edge is predicted where the probability exceeds one half. Average precision ranks every pair by its probability and needs no threshold; a model that cannot rank the pairs at all, whether it predicts no edge, every edge, or one half everywhere, scores the density there, which the result carries as flat_average_precision so the baseline is beside the number. Predicting no edge anywhere scores zero on precision, recall and F1.

Decode from the network latent mean, as above, rather than from a draw, for the same reason inference uses the latent mean: the same model over the same data should give the same network twice. For the full model the decoder and the latent are lists, one per tissue.

docs.title: Clustering
docs.text:
from preffect.clustering import clustering_recovery, resolution_for_target

grouping = resolution_for_target(result.latent.numpy(), target_clusters=5, seed=0)
print(grouping.n_clusters, "clusters at resolution", grouping.resolution)

scores = clustering_recovery(grouping, subtypes)   # subtypes from adata.obs
print(scores)
# adjusted Rand 0.412, adjusted mutual information 0.389
# (5 clusters against 5 known groups, 528 samples)

Both scores are corrected for chance. That matters at these sizes: with five groups and a few hundred samples, an uncorrected Rand index sits near 0.7 for a random grouping and reads as success.

target_clusters is a ceiling, not a promise. The search only lowers the resolution, so it stops as soon as the count is low enough and can return fewer. If it runs out of room, grouping.hit_the_floor is true and grouping.resolution is the resolution the labels actually came from.

docs.title: Figures
docs.text:
Every figure returns a matplotlib Figure and none of them write a file.

from preffect import plots

figure = plots.library_size_and_dispersion(result, counts)
plots.save_figure(figure, "figures/diagnostics.png")

plots.save_figure(
    plots.subtype_heatmap(counts, gene_names, subtypes, normalise="log_z_score"),
    "figures/pam50.png",
)

Available: library_size_histogram, gene_scatter, batch_adjustment, zero_fraction_against_pi, library_size_and_dispersion, latent_umap, loss_curves, subtype_heatmap.

Two things to know:

  • The UMAP is seeded, so the same model and data draw the same picture every run. Seeding costs parallelism, which UMAP will warn about; a figure you cannot reproduce is not worth the time it saved.
  • subtype_heatmap finds the PAM50 genes whichever way your data names them, symbols or Ensembl identifiers, and raises if it finds too few rather than drawing an empty figure.

docs.title: Choosing genes
docs.text:
from preffect.data.selection import apply_gene_selection, choose_genes
from preffect.gene_sets import PAM50

selection = choose_genes(tissues[0], n_genes=2000, force_genes=PAM50)
tissues = apply_gene_selection(tissues, selection, "training")

Genes are ranked by interquartile range, most variable first. force_genes keeps a panel regardless of its variability.

Choose genes once, from the training data, and apply the same selection to every split by name. Re-choosing per split gives different genes for the same column, which is a leak and a silent one.

docs.title: When things go wrong
docs.text:
Everything raises PreffectError or one of its subclasses, and the message names the setting, what was asked for, and what to do instead.

from preffect.errors import ConfigError, DataError, PreffectError

If a message tells you only that something is wrong and not what to do about it, that is a defect in the message; please report it.

docs.title: Speed, version 0.1 against version 0.2
docs.text:
Measured 2026-10-16. Forward pass, backward pass and one optimiser step, on 500 samples by 2,000 genes, with one correction variable. Median of three runs, 20 steps each, on a machine whose load average was between 130 and 180 throughout, with the two versions run interleaved so they met the same conditions.

Reproduce with tools/benchmark_v01.py and tools/benchmark_v02.py.

The two versions ran on different PyTorch versions, 0.1 on torch 2.5.1 and 0.2 on torch 2.14.1, because 0.1's environment is Python 3.9 and 0.2 needs torch 2.6 or later. This page did not say so until 2026-10-27. The same-version comparison is below, and it changes the conclusion.

The first version of this page left the network reconstruction out of the stand-in objective, so the graph models' network decoder was never exercised. That is the one place the two versions differ structurally, so the numbers below include it and the earlier ones understated version 0.2.

docs.title: CPU, eight threads
docs.text: model 0.1 0.2 simple 19.7 ms 23.6 ms 0.2 is 1.20x slower single 92.3 ms 113.1 ms 0.2 is 1.23x slower full 167.9 ms 202.7 ms 0.2 is 1.21x slower

docs.title: One A100 GPU
docs.text: model 0.1 0.2 simple 6.3 ms 4.6 ms 0.2 is 1.4x faster single 14.1 ms 16.6 ms 0.2 is 1.18x slower full 23.0 ms 23.0 ms the same

docs.title: Where version 0.2 is genuinely faster
docs.text:
The sample-sample network decoder, and by a wide margin. Version 0.1 reconstructs the network with a linear layer whose output width is the batch size; version 0.2 takes an inner product of the latent with itself and has no parameters there at all. At 500 samples, one full step of that component alone:

time parameters 0.1, Linear(128 -> 500) then sigmoid 1035 us 64,500 0.2, sigmoid(z @ z.T) 294 us 0

3.5x faster, with nothing to train. It also stops the architecture changing when the batch size changes, which was finding 20.

Including this component narrowed the overall CPU gap from about 1.35x to about 1.21x, which is the size of win it is worth: real, but a small part of a step dominated by the gene-wide matmuls both versions share.

docs.title: What this said, and what was wrong with it
docs.text: The first version of this section said version 0.2 was about a third slower than version 0.1 on a CPU, that the rewrite had cost roughly 35% of the speed, and that why had not been investigated. It stood for eleven days. It compared version 0.1 on torch 2.5.1 with version 0.2 on torch 2.14.1, and the difference it measured is the PyTorch version's, not the rewrite's. Finding 46.

docs.title: Measured on the same PyTorch, 2026-10-27
docs.text:
Version 0.2's benchmark run under torch 2.5.1, in a throwaway environment with the package's torch floor bypassed, interleaved with version 0.1 and with version 0.2 on torch 2.14.1 in the same minute. Simple model, 500 samples by 2,000 genes, load average about 130, medians of three:

threads 0.1 on torch 2.5.1 0.2 on torch 2.5.1 0.2 on torch 2.14.1 8 16.4 ms 13.1 ms 19.5 ms 1 44.5 ms 45.8 ms 47.8 ms

On the same PyTorch the rewrite is level or faster, which is what 6.7x fewer parameters would predict. On torch 2.14.1 it is slower, and only when there are threads to use. One component is identified: nn.Dropout on a hidden-sized tensor costs 0.07 to 0.11 ms under torch 2.5.1 and 0.65 to 0.85 ms under 2.14.1, seven times slower, and a random-number kernel does not parallelise; three dropouts a step is about 2 ms of the 6 ms gap. The rest is issue #24. On a GPU the two versions are within ten per cent of each other, which is to say indistinguishable at this precision.

tools/profile_step.py runs either version's step under the profiler, and its --control times plain layers of the same shapes with no PREFFECT code in them, which is how the PyTorch version was separated from the model.

docs.title: Where it entered, and what to do
docs.text:
A sweep of the CPU wheel of every release from 2.6.0 to 2.14.1 puts the change between 2.6.0 and 2.7.1: a dropout mask on 500 by 128 costs 0.09 ms at 2.6.0 and 0.55 to 0.83 ms at every release after. A per-operator profile of 0.2's step says dropout is a third of the 4 ms difference, zero_grad a tenth, and the rest a 10 to 40 per cent increase across ordinary kernels. The tables are in the development record, the decision of 2026-10-27 on installing PyTorch 2.6 on a CPU.

On a machine without a GPU, install PyTorch 2.6 before PREFFECT. It is the package's floor, so nothing is lost, and 0.2's step runs at 16.1 ms on it against 20.1 ms on 2.14.1 under the same conditions. Getting started gives the command.

model 0.1 parameters 0.2 parameters simple 5,350,973 800,414 0.2 is 6.7x smaller single 9,956,350 9,058,496 0.9x full 19,277,480 17,598,484 0.9x

The simple model's difference is finding 8: version 0.1 allocates layers the chosen model never uses, including a graph attention layer of several million parameters inside a model with no graph. Those layers cost memory and initialisation time but are never executed, which is why removing them shrinks the model without making it faster.

docs.title: The GPU is worth using
docs.text:
For version 0.2, one A100 against eight CPU threads:

model speed-up simple 5.0x single 8.8x full 7.0x

The graph models gain most, which is what you would expect from attention.

docs.title: What this measurement is not
docs.text:
It times the computation, not a complete run. Version 0.1's session machinery cannot be driven without writing files, so comparing whole runs would compare file handling as much as arithmetic. It also uses a stand-in objective, the sum of the fitted means, because version 0.1's loss needs its session state. Both versions get the same treatment, so the comparison is fair, but neither number is "how long my analysis takes".

Thread count matters separately and is covered in getting started.

docs.title: A worked example
docs.text: Fit a model, check it, apply it to data it has never seen, and score what it filled in. About three minutes end to end.

docs.title: The data
docs.text:
This step writes a small simulated cohort to work on, and says what it wrote.

.venv/bin/preffect example-data --out vignette_data

wrote vignette_data
  simple:
    train       120 samples  md5 4091e1ae
    validation   40 samples  md5 51f7b50a
    test         40 samples  md5 073eb2ee
  single:
    train       120 samples  md5 8ae37503
    validation   40 samples  md5 69d0f1e8
    test         40 samples  md5 2778a063
  full:
    train       120 samples  md5 fed1a84d  2 tissues
    validation   40 samples  md5 d0f02ad3  2 tissues
    test         40 samples  md5 42a999d2  2 tissues

200 genes, 3 groups, negative binomial counts.
No sample appears in more than one split, and the three files differ.
The genes are drawn once per cohort, so every split is the same genes.
Batch B has 40 of the 200 genes raised 1.3 times, for the correction variables to take out.
Every file carries the count each entry was drawn from in layers['true_expected_counts'].
The full model's two tissues are the same patients under different names.

Three splits, no sample in any two of them, and three different files. The command checks both before it reports success and refuses to write otherwise.

The checksums above are from the Python 3.12 library stack. The counts, the names and the batch labels are the same on Python 3.11, which resolves an older anndata and an older pandas, but the bytes those libraries write around them are not, so the checksums there differ. Compare them against another run of your own install, not against this page.

The counts are simulated from a negative binomial, which is what PREFFECT models, with three groups of samples that each raise a different block of genes. So there is something real to find, and you can tell whether the model found it.

The three splits are the same genes. Each gene has one level and one amount of noise, drawn once for the whole cohort, and every split is drawn from those. Without that a model fitted on the training split has nothing to say about the test split, however well it fits.

Batch B's own genes are raised, by a factor of 1.3, in a fifth of the genes picked at random and listed in the file under uns['batch_shifted_genes']. It is deliberately smaller than the four-fold lift the groups give their blocks, so the groups still dominate and the batch is the second thing you see. What it is there for is the correction variables, which take a known nuisance label out of what the encoder is given and are asked for from Python rather than from the command line (using it shows where), and the batch figure in the interface. It is not a demonstration of the objective's batch-centroid term, which no run here reaches: training passes no batch labels to the loss, so that term never fires.

Every file also carries the count each entry was drawn from, in layers['true_expected_counts']. That is the negative binomial mean, before the draw added its noise. No real cohort can have it; it is here so that step 4 can score a filled-in entry against what the entry should have been rather than against one noisy draw of it.

docs.title: 1. Check the data first
docs.text:
This step reads the files and says what is in them, before anything is fitted.

.venv/bin/preffect check --train vignette_data/simple/train \
                         --validation vignette_data/simple/validation

training: 1 tissue(s) from vignette_data/simple/train
  tissue 1: 120 samples, 200 genes, no network
  tissue 1: carries the count each entry was drawn from in layers['true_expected_counts'], so these counts are simulated
  the counts look usable
validation: 40 samples from vignette_data/simple/validation
  tissue 1: 0 of 120 training samples reappear in validation

The last line is the one to read. On your own data it tells you whether your splits are what you think they are. The line above it will not appear on your own data: only something simulated can carry the count each entry was drawn from, so finding it is how check tells you the file was generated rather than measured.

docs.title: 2. Fit
docs.text:
This step fits the model and stops it where it stops improving.

.venv/bin/preffect train --train vignette_data/simple/train \
                         --validation vignette_data/simple/validation \
                         --out model.pt \
                         --epochs 80 --batch-size 40 --seed 0 --threads 4 \
                         --patience 5

fitting a simple model: 200 genes, 36,090 parameters, 80 epochs
finished after 67 epoch(s)
  training loss   1218.02 -> 828.70
  validation loss 804.63
  stopped early, best epoch was 62
wrote model.pt

Validation close to training means it is not simply memorising, and here the two end within three per cent of each other. --patience 5 stops the run once the validation loss has not fallen for five epochs in a row, and the model written is the best epoch's, not the last. Here it fires at epoch 67 of a budget of 80 and keeps epoch 62, which is where more fitting stopped buying anything. A real cohort takes hundreds of epochs to settle, and the loss settling is not the whole story: see --patience on the command line page.

Where 80 epochs comes from

Fitted at four lengths on this data, on four threads of a CPU. The column headed test fit is the median across genes of the correlation between the model's expected counts and the actual counts of the 40 test samples, which is what this example exists to produce. With --patience 5 the runs budgeted 200 and 500 epochs both stop at 67 and give the 80-epoch row.

Budget Epochs run Training loss Validation loss Test fit Verdict 20 20 890.14 868.74 0.473 too short: the test counts are not reproduced 80 67, stopped early 828.70 804.63 0.784 the shortest that reproduces them 200 200 815.59 801.20 0.787 no better on the test split, three times the work 500 500 800.43 803.60 0.784 worse: the training loss keeps falling, the validation loss does not

Always pass --seed if you want the same model twice, and set --threads. The right number depends on the size of your data, and the default of 4 suits a small example rather than a real cohort. See getting started.

docs.title: 3. Apply it to data it has never seen
docs.text:
This step runs the fitted model over the test split and checks what came out.

.venv/bin/preffect apply --model model.pt \
                         --data vignette_data/simple/test \
                         --out cleaned.h5ad --threads 4

loaded a simple model written by PREFFECT 0.2.0, applying on cpu
matched 200 genes to the ones the model was fitted on
wrote cleaned.h5ad: 40 samples, 200 genes

cleaned.h5ad carries the adjusted counts in X, the predicted proportions in layers['composition'], and the latent summary in obsm['latent'].

This is the step the published figure got wrong. The test split was never seen during fitting and never used to decide when to stop, so what comes out is a genuine held-out result.

Two things are worth measuring on it. The first is whether the expected counts track the real ones: across the 40 test samples the median gene's correlation between the two is 0.78, and 162 of the 200 genes are above 0.5. The second is whether the latent summary has found the three groups, which the package will score for you. Clustering needs extra packages: pip install 'preffect[cluster]'.

import anndata as ad

from preffect.clustering import clustering_recovery, resolution_for_target

cleaned = ad.read_h5ad("cleaned.h5ad")
test = ad.read_h5ad("vignette_data/simple/test/counts.tau_1.h5ad")

found = resolution_for_target(cleaned.obsm["latent"], target_clusters=3, seed=0)
print(clustering_recovery(found.labels, test.obs["subtype"].astype(str)))
# adjusted Rand 1.000, adjusted mutual information 1.000
# (3 clusters against 3 known groups, 40 samples)

Both scores are corrected for chance, so 1.000 means the clustering of the latent space is the known grouping exactly, on samples the model never saw.

docs.title: 4. Score what it filled in
docs.text:
This step hides a fifth of the training entries, fits again on what is left, and scores the hidden entries against the counts they were drawn from.

.venv/bin/preffect train --train vignette_data/simple/train \
                         --validation vignette_data/simple/validation \
                         --out imputing.pt --hide 0.2 \
                         --epochs 80 --batch-size 40 --seed 0 --threads 4 \
                         --patience 5

hiding 20% of the training entries; the model is scored against the full counts
fitting a simple model: 200 genes, 36,090 parameters, 80 epochs
finished after 80 epoch(s)
  training loss   1160.82 -> 826.56
  validation loss 805.03
  imputation error on hidden entries 0.646, over 4,747 entries (53 hidden entries with a true value of zero left out)
wrote imputing.pt

That 0.646 is the average relative distance from the count that was observed, and most of it is noise rather than error: a count is one draw from a negative binomial, and nothing can predict the draw. Scoring against the mean it was drawn from instead separates the two, and on simulated data that mean is in the file.

from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import torch

from preffect.checkpoint import load_checkpoint
from preffect.inference import imputation_error, infer
from preffect.workflow import build_model, hide_entries, read_split, to_model_data

checkpoint = load_checkpoint("imputing.pt")
model = build_model(
    checkpoint.model_config.kind, checkpoint.n_genes, checkpoint.model_config, 1
)
model.load_state_dict(checkpoint.model_state)
model.eval()

# The same entries the run hid: the fraction and the seed are what choose them.
tissues = read_split(Path("vignette_data/simple/train"), 1)
data = hide_entries(to_model_data(tissues, checkpoint.model_config, False), 0.2, 0)
truth = torch.from_numpy(
    np.asarray(tissues[0].layers["true_expected_counts"], dtype=np.float32)
)

scores = imputation_error(
    infer(model, data).expected_counts, truth,
    hidden=torch.from_numpy(data.mask.hidden), kind="mean_relative",
)
print(round(scores["hidden"], 4), round(scores["visible"], 4))
# 0.1232 0.1279

So the model lands within about 12 per cent of what each hidden entry should have been, against 65 per cent of the single count that was actually drawn. The two numbers are the same measure on different comparisons, and the gap between them is the negative binomial noise. Nothing is skipped here: a true expected count is never zero, while 53 of the observed counts at hidden entries were, and a relative error cannot be computed against zero.

Your own data has no such layer, and PREFFECT will not invent one. On a real cohort the honest comparison is the observed count, which is the 0.646 above. Using it says more about what that number does and does not measure.

docs.title: If your cohort is too small to divide
docs.text:
This section is for a cohort that cannot give up samples to a validation set.

Leave --validation out. PREFFECT says so rather than inventing one:

validation: none given, so no validation loss will be reported

That is honest. Splitting 40 samples three ways gives you nothing you can trust, and copying one split into another gives you a number that looks like a held-out result and is not.

docs.title: The graph model
docs.text:
This section fits the model that reads a sample-sample network as well as the counts.

vignette_data/single/ carries the same thing plus a sample-sample network with real edges in it.

.venv/bin/preffect check --train vignette_data/single/train
#   tissue 1: 120 samples, 200 genes, a network with 240 edge(s), 4.0 per sample

.venv/bin/preffect train --train vignette_data/single/train --kind single \
                         --out single.pt --epochs 40 --batch-size 40 \
                         --seed 0 --threads 4

fitting a single model: 200 genes, 397,530 parameters, 40 epochs
finished after 40 epoch(s)
  training loss   526.47 -> 428.39
wrote single.pt

Check your network has edges before fitting a graph model

check reports the edge count because a file can carry a network that links every sample only to itself, which is a network with no edges at all. A graph model on one of those costs about ten times the parameters of the simple model and has nothing to attend to, so train refuses it.

docs.title: preffect.clustering
docs.text:
Group samples, and measure how well the grouping recovers known labels.

This is what the paper's subtype figures rest on, and what issues #4, #5 and

docs.title: 16 need. Finding 30 established that a KL divergence cannot rank two models,
docs.text:
because it moves under a rescaling that leaves every prediction identical. A clustering-recovery score does not move under that rescaling, which is why it is the measure those issues now ask for.

Three things can be clustered, and version 0.1 had a separate function for each with the resolution search copied into all three:

  • the latent space, the model's summary of each sample
  • the cleaned counts, what the model predicts each sample should look like
  • the observed counts, as a baseline to beat

Here there is one function and a choice of input, because three copies of a search is three places for it to go wrong, and in version 0.1 it had.

Clustering needs extra packages. pip install 'preffect[cluster]'. They are kept out of the core install because fitting a model does not need them.

docs.text:
A grouping of samples, and the settings that produced it.

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class ClusterResult:
    """A grouping of samples, and the settings that produced it."""

    #: One integer per sample, in the order the samples were given.
    labels: np.ndarray
    #: The resolution the labels were actually produced at. See ``cluster_samples``.
    resolution: float
    n_clusters: int
    source: str
    #: True when the search stopped without reaching the requested count.
    hit_the_floor: bool = False
    #: Each resolution tried and how many clusters it gave, oldest first.
    search: tuple[tuple[float, int], ...] = field(default=())

    def __post_init__(self) -> None:
        if self.labels.ndim != 1:
            raise PreffectError(
                f"labels should be one per sample, got shape {self.labels.shape}"
            )

    def __len__(self) -> int:
        return int(self.labels.shape[0])

docs.text:
How well a grouping recovers labels that were known in advance.

Every score here is unchanged by relabelling the clusters, which matters because cluster 0 has no meaning: a grouping that is right but numbered differently must not be penalised.

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class RecoveryScores:
    """How well a grouping recovers labels that were known in advance.

    Every score here is unchanged by relabelling the clusters, which matters
    because cluster 0 has no meaning: a grouping that is right but numbered
    differently must not be penalised.
    """

    adjusted_rand: float
    adjusted_mutual_information: float
    n_clusters: int
    n_true_groups: int
    n_samples: int

    def __str__(self) -> str:
        return (
            f"adjusted Rand {self.adjusted_rand:.3f}, "
            f"adjusted mutual information {self.adjusted_mutual_information:.3f} "
            f"({self.n_clusters} clusters against {self.n_true_groups} known groups, "
            f"{self.n_samples} samples)"
        )

docs.title: resolution_for_target
docs.text:
resolution_for_target(
    values: ndarray,
    *,
    target_clusters: int = 5,
    n_neighbors: int = 10,
    seed: int = 0,
    start: float = 1.0,
) -> ClusterResult

Lower the Leiden resolution until the grouping has few enough clusters.

Leiden does not take a number of clusters, it takes a resolution, and coarser groupings need lower numbers. Version 0.1 searched downward from 1.0 for a resolution giving at most five clusters, which is the number of PAM50 subtypes, and this keeps that behaviour with three corrections.

Version 0.1 reported a resolution its labels did not come from. When the search bottomed out it did this::

elif resolution <= 0.01:
    resolution = 0.1
    break

It set the variable and broke without re-running Leiden, so the labels still came from a resolution at or below 0.01 while 0.1 was what got recorded. Here the search returns the resolution the labels were actually produced at, and says separately whether it ran out of room.

The steps are taken on a grid, not by repeated subtraction. Version 0.1 did resolution -= 0.1 from 1.0, which reaches 0.30000000000000004 and then 0.20000000000000004, which is not <= 0.2, so the branch meant to switch to finer steps fired one step later than intended and at a value no one would predict.

At most, not exactly. The search only ever lowers the resolution, so it stops the moment the count is low enough and can return far fewer clusters than asked for, including one. That was true of version 0.1 too; what is new is that the result says so. target_clusters is a ceiling.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default values ndarray

samples by features.

required target_clusters int

the most clusters wanted.

5 n_neighbors int

neighbours per sample when building the graph.

10 seed int

passed to Leiden, which is otherwise not repeatable.

0 start float

the first resolution tried.

1.0 Source code in src/preffect/clustering.py 
def resolution_for_target(
    values: np.ndarray,
    *,
    target_clusters: int = 5,
    n_neighbors: int = 10,
    seed: int = 0,
    start: float = 1.0,
) -> ClusterResult:
    """Lower the Leiden resolution until the grouping has few enough clusters.

    Leiden does not take a number of clusters, it takes a resolution, and
    coarser groupings need lower numbers. Version 0.1 searched downward from 1.0
    for a resolution giving at most five clusters, which is the number of PAM50
    subtypes, and this keeps that behaviour with three corrections.

    **Version 0.1 reported a resolution its labels did not come from.** When the
    search bottomed out it did this::

        elif resolution <= 0.01:
            resolution = 0.1
            break

    It set the variable and broke *without re-running Leiden*, so the labels
    still came from a resolution at or below 0.01 while 0.1 was what got
    recorded. Here the search returns the resolution the labels were actually
    produced at, and says separately whether it ran out of room.

    **The steps are taken on a grid, not by repeated subtraction.** Version 0.1
    did ``resolution -= 0.1`` from 1.0, which reaches 0.30000000000000004 and
    then 0.20000000000000004, which is not ``<= 0.2``, so the branch meant to
    switch to finer steps fired one step later than intended and at a value no
    one would predict.

    **At most, not exactly.** The search only ever lowers the resolution, so it
    stops the moment the count is low enough and can return far fewer clusters
    than asked for, including one. That was true of version 0.1 too; what is
    new is that the result says so. ``target_clusters`` is a ceiling.

    :param values: samples by features.
    :param target_clusters: the most clusters wanted.
    :param n_neighbors: neighbours per sample when building the graph.
    :param seed: passed to Leiden, which is otherwise not repeatable.
    :param start: the first resolution tried.
    """
    import warnings

    import anndata as ad

    sc = _require_cluster_extras()

    if target_clusters < 1:
        raise PreffectError(f"target_clusters has to be at least 1, got {target_clusters}")
    values = np.ascontiguousarray(np.asarray(values, dtype=np.float32))
    if values.ndim != 2:
        raise PreffectError(f"expected samples by features, got shape {values.shape}")
    n_samples = values.shape[0]
    if n_samples < 2:
        raise PreffectError(f"clustering needs at least 2 samples, got {n_samples}")

    adata = ad.AnnData(values)
    with warnings.catch_warnings():
        warnings.simplefilter("ignore")
        # Never ask for more neighbours than there are other samples.
        sc.pp.neighbors(adata, n_neighbors=min(n_neighbors, n_samples - 1), use_rep="X")

        resolution = start
        search: list[tuple[float, int]] = []
        while True:
            sc.tl.leiden(
                adata,
                resolution=resolution,
                key_added="leiden",
                flavor="igraph",
                n_iterations=2,
                directed=False,
                random_state=seed,
            )
            labels = adata.obs["leiden"].to_numpy().astype(int)
            n_clusters = int(np.unique(labels).size)
            # The raw value, not a rounded copy of it. Rounding here made the
            # test that checks the steps land on a grid unable to fail: it read
            # back a number this line had already rounded. The grid is kept by
            # the step below, so an honest record shows it working.
            # Finding 37.
            search.append((resolution, n_clusters))

            if n_clusters <= target_clusters:
                hit_the_floor = False
                break
            if resolution <= MIN_RESOLUTION:
                # Out of room. Keep the labels this resolution produced rather
                # than reporting a resolution that was never run.
                hit_the_floor = True
                break
            # A grid, so every step lands on a value that can be written down.
            step = 0.01 if resolution <= 0.2 else 0.1
            resolution = round(max(MIN_RESOLUTION, resolution - step), 4)

    return ClusterResult(
        labels=labels,
        resolution=round(resolution, 4),
        n_clusters=n_clusters,
        source="values",
        hit_the_floor=hit_the_floor,
        search=tuple(search),
    )

def cluster_samples(
    result,
    source: Source = "latent",
    *,
    observed: np.ndarray | None = None,
    target_clusters: int = 5,
    n_neighbors: int = 10,
    seed: int = 0,
) -> ClusterResult:
    """Cluster what a fitted model produced, or the counts it started from.

    Replaces version 0.1's ``cluster_latent_space``, ``cluster_counts`` and
    ``cluster_true_counts``, which were three copies of one procedure differing
    only in the matrix they read.

    :param result: an ``InferenceResult`` from ``preffect.inference.infer``.
    :param source: ``latent``, ``cleaned_counts``, or ``observed_counts``.
    :param observed: required for ``observed_counts``, which is the baseline
        the model is supposed to beat and is not part of the model's output.
    """
    if source == "latent":
        values = result.latent.detach().cpu().numpy()
    elif source == "cleaned_counts":
        values = result.expected_counts.detach().cpu().numpy()
    elif source == "observed_counts":
        if observed is None:
            raise PreffectError(
                "clustering the observed counts needs them passed in as "
                "`observed`; they are the input to the model, not its output"
            )
        values = np.asarray(
            observed.detach().cpu().numpy() if hasattr(observed, "detach") else observed
        )
    else:
        raise PreffectError(
            f"source should be 'latent', 'cleaned_counts' or 'observed_counts', "
            f"got {source!r}"
        )

    found = resolution_for_target(
        values,
        target_clusters=target_clusters,
        n_neighbors=n_neighbors,
        seed=seed,
    )
    return ClusterResult(
        labels=found.labels,
        resolution=found.resolution,
        n_clusters=found.n_clusters,
        source=source,
        hit_the_floor=found.hit_the_floor,
        search=found.search,
    )

docs.title: clustering_recovery
docs.text:
clustering_recovery(labels, truth) -> RecoveryScores

Score a grouping against labels that were known in advance.

This is the functional measure issues #4, #5 and #16 ask for. Unlike a KL divergence it is unchanged by rescaling the latent space, so it compares two models rather than two gauges. See finding 30.

Both scores are corrected for chance, which matters at these sizes: with five groups and a few hundred samples an uncorrected Rand index sits near 0.7 for a random grouping and reads as success.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default labels

what the clustering produced, or a ClusterResult.

required truth

the known group of each sample. Any labels; they are matched by identity, not by value, so strings are fine.

required Source code in src/preffect/clustering.py 
def clustering_recovery(labels, truth) -> RecoveryScores:
    """Score a grouping against labels that were known in advance.

    This is the functional measure issues #4, #5 and #16 ask for. Unlike a KL
    divergence it is unchanged by rescaling the latent space, so it compares
    two models rather than two gauges. See finding 30.

    Both scores are corrected for chance, which matters at these sizes: with
    five groups and a few hundred samples an uncorrected Rand index sits near
    0.7 for a random grouping and reads as success.

    :param labels: what the clustering produced, or a ``ClusterResult``.
    :param truth: the known group of each sample. Any labels; they are matched
        by identity, not by value, so strings are fine.
    """
    try:
        from sklearn.metrics import adjusted_mutual_info_score, adjusted_rand_score
    except ImportError as error:  # pragma: no cover - exercised by hand
        raise PreffectError(
            "scoring a clustering needs scikit-learn, which is not installed. "
            "Run: pip install 'preffect[cluster]'"
        ) from error

    found = np.asarray(labels.labels if isinstance(labels, ClusterResult) else labels)
    known = np.asarray(truth)
    if found.shape[0] != known.shape[0]:
        raise PreffectError(
            f"there are {found.shape[0]} cluster labels and {known.shape[0]} "
            f"known labels; they have to match"
        )
    if found.shape[0] == 0:
        raise PreffectError("there is nothing to score")

    return RecoveryScores(
        adjusted_rand=float(adjusted_rand_score(known, found)),
        adjusted_mutual_information=float(
            adjusted_mutual_info_score(known, found)
        ),
        n_clusters=int(np.unique(found).size),
        n_true_groups=int(np.unique(known).size),
        n_samples=int(found.shape[0]),
    )

docs.title: preffect.plots
docs.text:
Figures for looking at what a fitted model did.

These are diagnostics, not publication figures: they are for deciding whether a run worked. Every one returns a matplotlib Figure and none of them write a file or open a window. Saving is a separate step, so a caller chooses where things land rather than inheriting one machine's paths. Version 0.1 shipped absolute paths as defaults and they reached a published figure.

Three things are deliberately different from version 0.1's six visualize_* methods:

Genes are named, not counted. Version 0.1's scatter plot drew for x in range(0, 50), which is column positions 0 to 49. Gene order in the matrix is whatever the file or the gene selection produced, so the figure showed an arbitrary subset that changed when the order did, and it raised IndexError below 50 genes. Here you pass gene names, and the default is the most variable genes, which is a stated rule rather than an accident of layout.

The UMAP is seeded. Version 0.1 built umap.UMAP(metric="cosine", n_neighbors=30) with no random_state in the one figure that goes in a paper, while seeding other UMAP calls in the same tree. UMAP is stochastic, so the same model and data gave a different picture every run.

The figures do not reach into a model. They take what inference returned plus the counts, so a figure can be drawn from a saved result without rebuilding anything.

Needs pip install 'preffect[viz]'.

def save_figure(figure: Figure, path) -> None:
    """Write a figure, creating the folder if it is missing.

    Separate from drawing on purpose. A function that draws *and* saves cannot
    be used to build a panel of several, and has to be told a path it should
    not have an opinion about.
    """
    from pathlib import Path

    path = Path(path)
    path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    figure.savefig(path, dpi=150)

Observed library sizes against what the model inferred.

The library size is the total counts in a sample. If the model's inferred sizes sit on top of the observed ones, it has learned the depth of sequencing; if they are shifted or much narrower, it has not.

def library_size_histogram(result, observed) -> Figure:
    """Observed library sizes against what the model inferred.

    The library size is the total counts in a sample. If the model's inferred
    sizes sit on top of the observed ones, it has learned the depth of
    sequencing; if they are shifted or much narrower, it has not.
    """
    figure, axes = _figure(1, 2)
    observed_totals = _as_array(observed).sum(axis=1)
    inferred_totals = _as_array(result.library_size).ravel()

    for axis, values, title, colour in (
        (axes[0][0], observed_totals, "Observed", "tab:blue"),
        (axes[0][1], inferred_totals, "Inferred by the model", "tab:orange"),
    ):
        axis.hist(values, bins=30, color=colour, edgecolor="white")
        axis.set_title(title)
        axis.set_xlabel("total counts in a sample")
        axis.set_ylabel("samples")

    # Same limits on both, or two different pictures look like the same one.
    both = np.concatenate([observed_totals, inferred_totals])
    for axis in (axes[0][0], axes[0][1]):
        axis.set_xlim(both.min(), both.max())
    return figure

def observed_library_sizes(observed) -> Figure:
    """How deeply each sample was sequenced, before any model is fitted.

    One histogram of the library sizes, which are each sample's total count:
    the left panel of :func:`library_size_histogram`, for a folder that has
    not been fitted yet. A sample far deeper or far shallower than the rest
    pulls a fit towards itself, and this is the moment to see it.

    :param observed: the counts, samples by genes.
    """
    totals = _as_array(observed).sum(axis=1)
    if totals.size == 0:
        raise PreffectError("there are no samples to draw")
    figure, axes = _figure(1, 1, size=(6.0, 3.6))
    axes[0][0].hist(totals, bins=min(30, max(5, totals.size // 2)),
                    color="tab:blue", edgecolor="white")
    axes[0][0].set_xlabel("total counts in a sample")
    axes[0][0].set_ylabel("samples")
    return figure

def gene_scatter(
    result,
    observed,
    *,
    gene_names: Sequence[str] | None = None,
    genes: Sequence[str] | None = None,
    n_genes: int = 12,
) -> Figure:
    """Observed against fitted counts, one panel per gene.

    A gene whose points lie on the diagonal is one the model reproduces.

    :param genes: which genes to draw, **by name**. Defaults to the most
        variable, because those are the ones a model can be wrong about. Version
        0.1 drew columns 0 to 49, which is a different set of genes every time
        the gene order changes.
    :param gene_names: names for the columns, needed to select by name.
    """
    observed_values = _as_array(observed)
    fitted = _as_array(result.expected_counts)
    if observed_values.shape != fitted.shape:
        raise PreffectError(
            f"observed counts are {observed_values.shape} and fitted are "
            f"{fitted.shape}; they have to match"
        )

    n_available = observed_values.shape[1]
    if genes is not None:
        if gene_names is None:
            raise PreffectError(
                "selecting genes by name needs `gene_names` for the columns"
            )
        lookup = {str(name): i for i, name in enumerate(gene_names)}
        missing = [g for g in genes if str(g) not in lookup]
        if missing:
            raise PreffectError(
                f"these genes are not in the data: {', '.join(map(str, missing[:5]))}"
            )
        chosen = np.array([lookup[str(g)] for g in genes])
    else:
        chosen = _most_variable(observed_values, min(n_genes, n_available))

    columns = min(4, len(chosen))
    rows = int(np.ceil(len(chosen) / columns))
    figure, axes = _figure(rows, columns, size=(3.0, 3.0))

    for position, column in enumerate(chosen):
        axis = axes[position // columns][position % columns]
        axis.scatter(observed_values[:, column], fitted[:, column], s=8, alpha=0.6)
        limit = max(observed_values[:, column].max(), fitted[:, column].max(), 1.0)
        axis.plot([0, limit], [0, limit], linestyle="--", linewidth=1, color="grey")
        label = str(gene_names[column]) if gene_names is not None else f"column {column}"
        axis.set_title(label, fontsize=9)
        axis.set_xlabel("observed")
        axis.set_ylabel("fitted")

    for empty in range(len(chosen), rows * columns):  # blank any unused panels
        axes[empty // columns][empty % columns].axis("off")
    return figure

def batch_adjustment(result, observed, batches) -> Figure:
    """Per-gene means of one batch against another, observed and fitted.

    If batch correction worked, the fitted panel is closer to the diagonal than
    the observed one: the model has removed a difference that was in the data.
    Every pair of batches is drawn, capped at the first ``MAX_BATCHES`` because
    the number of pairs grows as the square.
    """
    observed_values = _as_array(observed)
    fitted = _as_array(result.expected_counts)
    labels = _as_array(batches).ravel()
    if labels.shape[0] != observed_values.shape[0]:
        raise PreffectError(
            f"there are {labels.shape[0]} batch labels and "
            f"{observed_values.shape[0]} samples; they have to match"
        )

    present = list(dict.fromkeys(labels.tolist()))[:MAX_BATCHES]
    pairs = [(a, b) for i, a in enumerate(present) for b in present[i + 1 :]]
    if not pairs:
        raise PreffectError(
            f"batch comparison needs at least two batches, found {len(present)}"
        )

    figure, axes = _figure(len(pairs), 2, size=(4.0, 3.6))
    for row, (first, second) in enumerate(pairs):
        for column, (values, title) in enumerate(
            ((observed_values, "Observed"), (fitted, "Fitted"))
        ):
            axis = axes[row][column]
            x = values[labels == first].mean(axis=0)
            y = values[labels == second].mean(axis=0)
            axis.scatter(x, y, s=6, alpha=0.5)
            limit = max(x.max(), y.max(), 1.0)
            axis.plot([0, limit], [0, limit], linestyle="--", linewidth=1, color="grey")
            axis.set_title(f"{title}: batch {first} against {second}", fontsize=9)
            axis.set_xlabel(f"mean count, batch {first}")
            axis.set_ylabel(f"mean count, batch {second}")
    return figure

def zero_fraction_against_pi(result, observed) -> Figure:
    """How often a gene is zero, against the model's own zero probability.

    Only meaningful for the zero-inflated likelihood, which is the one with a
    separate probability of a structural zero. Refused otherwise rather than
    drawn empty: version 0.1's habit of quietly producing something was the
    most expensive thing in it.
    """
    if result.zero_logits is None:
        raise PreffectError(
            "this figure needs the zero-inflated likelihood (ZINB); the fitted "
            "model has no zero probability to plot. Refit with likelihood=ZINB."
        )

    observed_values = _as_array(observed)
    probability = 1.0 / (1.0 + np.exp(-_as_array(result.zero_logits)))

    figure, axes = _figure()
    axis = axes[0][0]
    axis.scatter(
        (observed_values == 0).mean(axis=0), probability.mean(axis=0), s=8, alpha=0.6
    )
    axis.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], linestyle="--", linewidth=1, color="grey")
    axis.set_xlabel("fraction of samples where the gene is zero")
    axis.set_ylabel("mean fitted probability of a zero")
    axis.set_xlim(0, 1)
    axis.set_ylim(0, 1)
    return figure

def library_size_and_dispersion(result, observed) -> Figure:
    """Four panels: gene means, dispersion, library size, and mean against dispersion.

    The last panel is the one worth looking at. In a negative binomial, the
    dispersion sets how much more variable the counts are than a Poisson would
    be, and it usually falls as the mean rises. A flat or rising relationship
    suggests the dispersion is not being fitted.
    """
    observed_values = _as_array(observed)
    fitted = _as_array(result.expected_counts)
    dispersion = _as_array(result.dispersion)

    figure, axes = _figure(2, 2, size=(4.5, 3.6))

    axes[0][0].scatter(
        observed_values.mean(axis=0), fitted.mean(axis=0), s=6, alpha=0.5
    )
    limit = max(observed_values.mean(axis=0).max(), fitted.mean(axis=0).max(), 1.0)
    axes[0][0].plot([0, limit], [0, limit], "--", linewidth=1, color="grey")
    axes[0][0].set_title("Gene means", fontsize=10)
    axes[0][0].set_xlabel("observed")
    axes[0][0].set_ylabel("fitted")

    axes[0][1].hist(dispersion.mean(axis=0), bins=30, color="tab:green", edgecolor="white")
    axes[0][1].set_title("Fitted dispersion per gene", fontsize=10)
    axes[0][1].set_xlabel("dispersion")
    axes[0][1].set_ylabel("genes")

    axes[1][0].scatter(
        observed_values.sum(axis=1), _as_array(result.library_size).ravel(), s=8, alpha=0.6
    )
    axes[1][0].set_title("Library size", fontsize=10)
    axes[1][0].set_xlabel("observed total")
    axes[1][0].set_ylabel("fitted total")

    mean_counts = np.clip(observed_values.mean(axis=0), 1e-8, None)
    axes[1][1].scatter(mean_counts, dispersion.mean(axis=0), s=6, alpha=0.5)
    axes[1][1].set_xscale("log")
    axes[1][1].set_yscale("log")
    axes[1][1].set_title("Mean against dispersion", fontsize=10)
    axes[1][1].set_xlabel("mean count (log scale)")
    axes[1][1].set_ylabel("dispersion (log scale)")
    return figure

The left panel is the fitted dispersion, which is how much more variable the counts are than pure counting noise would make them. The right panel, drawn only for the zero-inflated model, is the fitted probability that this gene's count is a structural zero, with a dashed line at the share of samples in which it was actually observed to be zero. def gene_dispersion_and_zeros(result, observed, *, gene_names, gene) -> Figure:
    """One gene's fitted dispersion across the samples, and its chance of a zero.

    Both quantities are fitted for every sample separately, so for a single
    gene each is a spread rather than a number, and the spread is the thing
    worth seeing: a dispersion that is the same in every sample says the model
    found the gene equally erratic throughout.

    The left panel is the fitted dispersion, which is how much more variable
    the counts are than pure counting noise would make them. The right panel,
    drawn only for the zero-inflated model, is the fitted probability that
    this gene's count is a structural zero, with a dashed line at the share of
    samples in which it was actually observed to be zero. The two should agree.

    :param gene_names: names for the columns, in order.
    :param gene: which gene to draw, by name.
    """
    observed_values = _as_array(observed)
    column = _gene_index(gene_names, gene)
    dispersion = _as_array(result.dispersion)[:, column]
    has_zeros = result.zero_logits is not None

    figure, axes = _figure(1, 2 if has_zeros else 1, size=(4.5, 3.6))
    axes[0][0].hist(dispersion, bins=20, color="tab:green", edgecolor="white")
    axes[0][0].set_title(f"{gene}: fitted dispersion", fontsize=10)
    axes[0][0].set_xlabel("dispersion")
    axes[0][0].set_ylabel("samples")

    if has_zeros:
        probability = 1.0 / (1.0 + np.exp(-_as_array(result.zero_logits)[:, column]))
        axes[0][1].hist(probability, bins=20, color="tab:purple", edgecolor="white")
        axes[0][1].axvline(
            float((observed_values[:, column] == 0).mean()),
            linestyle="--",
            linewidth=1,
            color="grey",
        )
        axes[0][1].set_title(f"{gene}: fitted chance of a zero", fontsize=10)
        axes[0][1].set_xlabel("probability of a structural zero")
        axes[0][1].set_ylabel("samples")
        axes[0][1].set_xlim(0, 1)
    return figure

def sample_fit_spread(
    scores,
    *,
    highlight: int | None = None,
    measure: str = "mean log probability per gene",
) -> Figure:
    """How one number per sample is spread over the cohort, with one sample marked.

    Takes the scores rather than computing them, so that a table of the same
    numbers and this figure cannot disagree about what they are. The dashed
    line is the sample asked about, and what it is for is placing that sample
    against the rest: a tail far to the left is the handful of samples the
    model cannot account for.

    :param scores: one value per sample.
    :param highlight: the position of one sample to mark, or ``None``.
    :param measure: what the scores are, for the axis label.
    """
    values = _as_array(scores).ravel()
    if values.size == 0:
        raise PreffectError("there are no sample scores to draw")

    figure, axes = _figure(1, 1, size=(6.0, 3.6))
    axes[0][0].hist(values, bins=min(30, max(5, values.size // 2)),
                    color="tab:blue", edgecolor="white")
    if highlight is not None:
        axes[0][0].axvline(
            float(values[highlight]), linestyle="--", linewidth=1.5, color="tab:red"
        )
    axes[0][0].set_xlabel(measure)
    axes[0][0].set_ylabel("samples")
    return figure

This is the figure the paper's subtype panels are built from, and it is the one version 0.1 left unseeded, so the same model and data drew a different picture every run. seed fixes that; pass seed=None deliberately if you want the old behaviour.

Seeding costs parallelism, and UMAP says so: it drops to one thread when given a random_state, because its parallel path is not deterministic. On a vignette this is invisible. On 528 samples it is worth knowing before you wonder why the figure is slow, and it is the trade this function makes on purpose: a figure you cannot reproduce is not worth the time it saved.

Replaces both visualize_latent_recons_umap and draw_umap_with_subtype: they differed only in what coloured the points.

def latent_umap(
    result,
    *,
    colour_by=None,
    colour_label: str = "group",
    seed: int = 0,
    n_neighbors: int = 30,
    metric: str = "cosine",
) -> Figure:
    """The latent space in two dimensions, optionally coloured by a known label.

    This is the figure the paper's subtype panels are built from, and it is the
    one version 0.1 left unseeded, so the same model and data drew a different
    picture every run. ``seed`` fixes that; pass ``seed=None`` deliberately if
    you want the old behaviour.

    **Seeding costs parallelism, and UMAP says so**: it drops to one thread
    when given a ``random_state``, because its parallel path is not
    deterministic. On a vignette this is invisible. On 528 samples it is worth
    knowing before you wonder why the figure is slow, and it is the trade this
    function makes on purpose: a figure you cannot reproduce is not worth the
    time it saved.

    Replaces both ``visualize_latent_recons_umap`` and
    ``draw_umap_with_subtype``: they differed only in what coloured the points.

    :param colour_by: one label per sample. Subtypes, batches, anything.
    """
    try:
        import umap
    except ImportError as error:  # pragma: no cover - exercised by hand
        raise PreffectError(
            "the UMAP figure needs umap-learn, which is not installed. "
            "Run: pip install 'preffect[viz]'"
        ) from error

    latent = _as_array(result.latent)
    n_samples = latent.shape[0]
    if n_samples < 3:
        raise PreffectError(f"a UMAP needs at least 3 samples, got {n_samples}")

    reducer = umap.UMAP(
        metric=metric,
        # Never ask for more neighbours than there are other samples. Version
        # 0.1 hardcoded 30 and failed on any cohort smaller than that.
        n_neighbors=min(n_neighbors, n_samples - 1),
        random_state=seed,
    )
    embedding = reducer.fit_transform(latent)

    figure, axes = _figure(size=(5.5, 4.5))
    axis = axes[0][0]
    if colour_by is None:
        axis.scatter(embedding[:, 0], embedding[:, 1], s=14, alpha=0.8)
    else:
        labels = _as_array(colour_by).ravel()
        if labels.shape[0] != n_samples:
            raise PreffectError(
                f"there are {labels.shape[0]} labels and {n_samples} samples; "
                f"they have to match"
            )
        for value in dict.fromkeys(labels.tolist()):
            rows = labels == value
            axis.scatter(
                embedding[rows, 0], embedding[rows, 1], s=14, alpha=0.8, label=str(value)
            )
        axis.legend(title=colour_label, fontsize=8, title_fontsize=9)

    axis.set_xlabel("UMAP 1")
    axis.set_ylabel("UMAP 2")
    # Said on the figure, because a UMAP's axes have no units and the distances
    # between well-separated clumps do not mean anything.
    axis.set_title(
        f"Latent space, UMAP (seed {seed}, {metric} distance)", fontsize=10
    )
    return figure

def loss_curves(history) -> Figure:
    """The objective over epochs, in total and term by term.

    Replaces ``plot_progression`` and ``plot_progression_all``. Validation is
    drawn on the same axes as training where it exists, because the gap between
    them is the thing worth seeing and two separate figures hide it.
    """
    epochs = [record.epoch for record in history.epochs]
    if not epochs:
        raise PreffectError("there are no epochs to draw")

    term_names = list(history.epochs[0].train.mean_terms)
    figure, axes = _figure(1, 2, size=(5.5, 4.0))

    axes[0][0].plot(epochs, history.train_losses, label="training", linewidth=2)
    validation = [
        record.validation.mean_loss if record.validation else None
        for record in history.epochs
    ]
    if any(v is not None for v in validation):
        drawn = [(e, v) for e, v in zip(epochs, validation, strict=True) if v is not None]
        axes[0][0].plot(
            [e for e, _ in drawn], [v for _, v in drawn], label="validation", linewidth=2
        )
        axes[0][0].legend(fontsize=9)
    axes[0][0].set_title("Objective", fontsize=10)
    axes[0][0].set_xlabel("epoch")
    axes[0][0].set_ylabel("mean loss per batch")

    for name in term_names:
        axes[0][1].plot(
            epochs,
            [record.train.mean_terms[name] for record in history.epochs],
            label=name,
            linewidth=1.5,
        )
    axes[0][1].set_yscale("symlog")
    axes[0][1].set_title("Each term (symmetric log scale)", fontsize=10)
    axes[0][1].set_xlabel("epoch")
    axes[0][1].set_ylabel("mean value per batch")
    axes[0][1].legend(fontsize=8)

    if history.stopped_early and history.best_epoch is not None:
        for axis in (axes[0][0], axes[0][1]):
            axis.axvline(
                history.best_epoch, linestyle=":", color="grey", linewidth=1
            )
    return figure

def subtype_heatmap(
    values,
    gene_names: Sequence[str],
    subtypes,
    *,
    gene_set=None,
    normalise: str = "z_score",
    subtype_order: Sequence[str] | None = None,
    min_genes: int = 10,
    title: str = "PAM50 genes by subtype",
) -> Figure:
    """Expression of the PAM50 genes, with samples grouped by subtype.

    This is the figure the paper's subtype panel is built from. Rows are
    samples, grouped and ordered by subtype with a colour bar on the left;
    columns are the genes of the set that are present in the data.

    Four things differ from version 0.1's ``create_PAM50_heatmap``, all of them
    finding 33.

    **The genes are found whichever way the data names them.** Version 0.1
    matched against a list of symbols, and three of the nine datasets name their
    genes with Ensembl identifiers. It matched nothing on those, printed
    ``PAM50 Genes Found: 0``, and drew a heatmap of an empty matrix. Here both
    namings are tried and the better match is used.

    **Too few matches is refused, not drawn.** ``min_genes`` is the floor.

    **Any number of subtypes works.** Version 0.1 indexed a hardcoded list of
    five colours by subtype, so a dataset with six categories raised
    ``IndexError``. Two of the nine have six: ``our_dcis`` has an explicit
    ``NaN`` group and GSE209998 has ``Claudin``.

    **Samples are ordered by subtype, not by colour name.** Version 0.1 sorted
    on the colour string it had assigned, so the groups came out in the
    alphabetical order of five colour names and changing a colour changed the
    figure.

    :param values: samples by genes. Counts, or a model's cleaned counts.
    :param normalise: ``z_score`` per gene, ``log_z_score`` for counts spanning
        orders of magnitude, or ``min_max`` to match version 0.1. Min-max is
        set by the single largest value in a gene, so one outlier flattens the
        rest; it is here for comparison, not because it is a good default.
    """
    from preffect.gene_sets import PAM50, match_genes

    gene_set = gene_set or PAM50
    matrix = np.nan_to_num(_as_array(values).astype(float))
    labels = _as_array(subtypes).ravel()

    if matrix.shape[0] != labels.shape[0]:
        raise PreffectError(
            f"there are {matrix.shape[0]} samples and {labels.shape[0]} subtype "
            f"labels; they have to match"
        )
    if matrix.shape[1] != len(gene_names):
        raise PreffectError(
            f"there are {matrix.shape[1]} columns and {len(gene_names)} gene "
            f"names; they have to match"
        )

    positions, found, naming = match_genes(gene_set, gene_names)
    if len(positions) < min_genes:
        raise PreffectError(
            f"only {len(positions)} of {len(gene_set)} {gene_set.name} genes are "
            f"in this data, which is below min_genes={min_genes}. Tried both "
            f"gene symbols and Ensembl identifiers. Check that the gene names "
            f"are what you think they are: this data names its first gene "
            f"{str(gene_names[0])!r}."
        )

    matrix = matrix[:, positions]
    if normalise == "z_score":
        spread = matrix.std(axis=0)
        scaled = (matrix - matrix.mean(axis=0)) / np.where(spread > 0, spread, 1.0)
    elif normalise == "log_z_score":
        logged = np.log1p(np.clip(matrix, 0, None))
        spread = logged.std(axis=0)
        scaled = (logged - logged.mean(axis=0)) / np.where(spread > 0, spread, 1.0)
    elif normalise == "min_max":
        low, high = matrix.min(axis=0), matrix.max(axis=0)
        scaled = (matrix - low) / np.where(high > low, high - low, 1.0)
    else:
        raise PreffectError(
            f"normalise should be 'z_score', 'log_z_score' or 'min_max', "
            f"got {normalise!r}"
        )

    groups = _ordered_groups(labels, subtype_order)
    row_order = np.concatenate([np.flatnonzero(labels == group) for group in groups])
    scaled = scaled[row_order]

    import matplotlib as mpl

    # A colour per subtype from a colormap, so any number of them works.
    palette = mpl.colormaps["tab10"].resampled(max(len(groups), 1))
    colour_of = {group: palette(i) for i, group in enumerate(groups)}

    from matplotlib.figure import Figure

    # Built by hand rather than through _figure, because the subtype bar is a
    # thin strip beside the heatmap, not a panel of equal width.
    figure = Figure(
        figsize=(max(8.0, 0.22 * len(found) + 4.0), 7.0), layout="constrained"
    )
    bar, main = figure.subplots(
        1, 2, gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1, 28], "wspace": 0.02}
    )

    bar.imshow(
        np.array([[colour_of[group] for group in labels[row_order]]]).transpose(1, 0, 2),
        aspect="auto",
        interpolation="nearest",
    )
    bar.set_xticks([])
    bar.set_yticks([])
    bar.set_ylabel(f"{len(row_order)} samples, grouped by subtype")

    limit = float(np.abs(scaled).max()) if normalise != "min_max" else 1.0
    image = main.imshow(
        scaled,
        aspect="auto",
        cmap="RdBu_r" if normalise != "min_max" else "hot",
        vmin=-limit if normalise != "min_max" else 0.0,
        vmax=limit,
        interpolation="nearest",
    )
    main.set_xticks(range(len(found)))
    main.set_xticklabels(found, rotation=90, fontsize=6)
    main.set_yticks([])
    main.set_title(f"{title} ({len(found)} genes matched by {naming}, {normalise})",
                   fontsize=10)

    figure.colorbar(image, ax=main, shrink=0.6, label=normalise.replace("_", " "))
    main.legend(
        handles=[
            mpl.patches.Patch(
                color=colour_of[group],
                label=f"{group} ({int((labels == group).sum())})",
            )
            for group in groups
        ],
        loc="center left",
        bbox_to_anchor=(1.18, 0.5),
        fontsize=8,
        title="subtype",
        title_fontsize=9,
    )
    return figure

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Everything a run needs, typed and checked before anything is built.

The settings are frozen once built, a bad combination raises with the setting named, and nothing is rewritten behind your back.

docs.title: preffect.config
docs.text:
PREFFECT configuration: typed, validated once, then frozen.

The previous version kept configuration in a single dictionary of about ninety untyped keys, imported as a module global and modified in place by the data loader, the batch iterator, the factory and the validation routine. Several defects came directly from that arrangement, and each rule below exists because of one of them. The rules are named in how_this_project_breaks.md.

Three properties this module guarantees:

  1. Nothing is silently rewritten. If a setting cannot be honoured, a :class:~preffect.errors.ConfigError says which setting, what was asked for, and what to do. The previous version would quietly change the model you asked for into a different one.
  2. Per-tissue weights are checked against the number of tissues. A list of the wrong length used to be accepted and then silently truncated, which dropped whole tissues out of the objective.
  3. Nothing has a filesystem default. Paths are supplied by the caller or the configuration does not build.

A configuration is immutable once constructed. To vary one setting, use :meth:PreffectConfig.replace, which re-runs every check.

class ModelKind(StrEnum):
    """Which of the three models to build.

    ``SIMPLE`` uses counts alone. ``SINGLE`` adds a sample-sample adjacency
    network for one tissue. ``FULL`` extends that to several matched tissues.
    """

    SIMPLE = "simple"
    SINGLE = "single"
    FULL = "full"

    @property
    def uses_adjacency(self) -> bool:
        return self is not ModelKind.SIMPLE

validation_path is optional, and that is deliberate. @dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True)
class DataConfig:
    """Where the counts are and how much of them to use.

    ``validation_path`` is optional, and that is deliberate. The previous
    version required a validation folder to exist before it would run, so a
    cohort too small to split was handled by putting the same file in both
    folders. The resulting "validation" loss was the training loss. Here,
    leaving it unset means no validation loss is computed and none is reported.
    """

    train_path: Path
    n_tissues: int = 1
    validation_path: Path | None = None
    test_path: Path | None = None
    select_genes: int | None = None
    select_samples: int | None = None
    masking: Masking = Masking.NONE
    mask_fraction: float = 0.0

    def __post_init__(self) -> None:
        object.__setattr__(self, "train_path", Path(self.train_path))
        for name in ("validation_path", "test_path"):
            value = getattr(self, name)
            if value is not None:
                object.__setattr__(self, name, Path(value))

        if not isinstance(self.masking, Masking):
            try:
                object.__setattr__(self, "masking", Masking(self.masking))
            except ValueError as exc:
                allowed = sorted(m.value for m in Masking)
                raise ConfigError(
                    f"masking must be one of {allowed}, got {self.masking!r}"
                ) from exc

        if self.n_tissues < 1:
            raise ConfigError(f"n_tissues must be at least 1, got {self.n_tissues}")

        for name in ("select_genes", "select_samples"):
            value = getattr(self, name)
            if value is not None and value < 1:
                raise ConfigError(f"{name} must be at least 1 when set, got {value}")

        if not 0.0 <= self.mask_fraction <= 1.0:
            raise ConfigError(
                f"mask_fraction is a proportion and must lie in [0, 1], got {self.mask_fraction}"
            )
        if self.masking is Masking.NONE and self.mask_fraction > 0:
            raise ConfigError(
                f"mask_fraction is {self.mask_fraction} but masking is 'none'. "
                "Set masking to 'MCAR' to mask counts, or set mask_fraction to 0."
            )
        if self.masking is not Masking.NONE and self.mask_fraction == 0:
            raise ConfigError(
                f"masking is {self.masking.value!r} but mask_fraction is 0, so nothing "
                "would be masked. Set a fraction above 0, or set masking to 'none'."
            )

    @property
    def has_validation(self) -> bool:
        return self.validation_path is not None
